emails.subject: Deadlines vs. schedules: which one is better for goal achievement?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I'm torn between the two.

On the one hand, I'm a big believer in setting deadlines when it comes to setting goals.

I think it's important to see our destination accompanied by a target date. It helps us to prioritize tasks. It also helps us to allocate our limited attentional resources (time, focus, etc.).

At the same time, I'm also a huge advocate of putting goal-oriented tasks on a schedule.

That way, we don't have to rely on willpower to do them. We simply note the time of day, check our schedule to see what we should be doing, and get to it.

Can these two tactics coexist?

There's a lot of talk about deadlines versus schedules, and which option leads to greater success.

Both tactics have their supporters and detractors. And some of these folks are pretty vehement about their opinions.

Here's the thing...

You don't need to choose. In my opinion, you should set deadlines AND schedules whenever you set goals.

Here's a personal example to show you how they work together:

I recently finishing writing my latest book (more details coming in a few weeks). Before I wrote the first word, I opened up a monthly calendar in Google Calendar. Then, I chose a target date by which I wanted to complete the first draft.

So far, so good.

Next, I created an action plan. I worked backward from the target date, and I determined how much I'd need to write each day to achieve my goal.

Finally, I scheduled writing time on my daily calendar. I decided to write from 5:30 a.m. to 7:30 a.m.

Every day. Monday through Sunday.

Can you guess what happened?

I finished the first draft by the target date. But here's the best part...

It wasn't difficult at all. I didn't need to rely on willpower to write. Nor did I need to "get motivated" or inspired or whisper affirmations to myself.

I simply looked at the clock each morning, saw that it was 5:30 a.m., and started writing.

The rest took care of itself.

That's how deadlines and schedules can work together to help you to achieve your goals.

Try the following...

Choose one of your goals. It doesn't matter whether it's to learn a new language, run a marathon, or write a novel. Any goal will do.

Open up Google Calendar and select a target date. Make sure it's practical given your available time.

Next, create an action plan to hit that date.

For example, let's say you want to learn a new language. Commit to listening for 30 minutes each day to podcasts that offer lessons in that language.

Finally, put that activity on your daily schedule. Try to schedule it at the same time each day.

After a couple weeks, you'll find yourself doing it as part of your daily routine. Easy peasy.

That's it for now.

Stay well and talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you're not sure how to set goals you'll actually achieve, check out my book The P.R.I.M.E.R. Goal Setting Method. It'll take you, step-by-step guide, through the entire process.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

我在這兩者之間猶豫不決。

一方面,在設定目標時,我非常相信「設定截止日期」的重要性。

我認為,看見目的地並搭配一個目標日期是很重要的。這有助於我們排定任務的優先順序,也有助於我們分配有限的注意力資源(時間、專注力等)。

但與此同時,我也十分提倡把以目標為導向的任務排進「行事曆」中。

這樣一來,我們就不必依賴意志力去完成它們。我們只需留意當下的時間,查看行事曆上該做什麼,然後去做就好。

這兩種做法能夠並存嗎?

關於截止日期與行事曆孰優孰劣,一直有很多討論。

這兩種做法都各有支持者與反對者。有些人對自己的看法還相當堅持。

事情是這樣的……

你不需要二選一。依我之見,設定目標時,你應該同時設定截止日期「與」行事曆。

這裡有一個親身經歷的例子,讓你看看它們是如何協同運作的:

我最近剛寫完我的新書(幾週後會有更多細節)。在寫下第一個字之前,我先在 Google 日曆中打開一個月曆。然後,我選定了一個希望完成初稿的目標日期。

到目前為止都還不錯。

接著,我制定了一個行動計畫。我從目標日期往回推算,確定每天需要寫多少字才能達成目標。

最後,我把寫作時間排進了每日行事曆。我決定從早上 5:30 寫到 7:30。

每天都是,週一到週日。

你猜發生了什麼事?

我在目標日期前完成了初稿。但最棒的部分是……

這一點都不困難。我不需要依賴意志力去寫作,也不需要「找動力」、尋求靈感,或對自己喃喃唸著肯定語句。

我只是每天早上看看時鐘,發現是 5:30,然後就開始寫作。

剩下的事情自然就水到渠成了。

這就是截止日期與行事曆如何協同運作,幫助你達成目標。

試試看以下做法……

選擇你的其中一個目標。無論是學一門新語言、跑一場馬拉松,還是寫一本小說,任何目標都可以。

打開 Google 日曆,選定一個目標日期。務必確保它在你可運用的時間內是切實可行的。

接著,制定一個能達成該日期的行動計畫。

舉例來說,假設你想學一門新語言,就承諾每天花 30 分鐘聽提供該語言課程的 Podcast。

最後,把這項活動排進你的每日行事曆。盡量每天在同一個時間安排它。

幾週之後,你會發現這已經成為你日常routine的一部分了。輕輕鬆鬆。

今天就談到這裡。

保重,咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你不確定該如何設定真正能達成的目標,可以看看我的書《The P.R.I.M.E.R. Goal Setting Method》。它會用逐步引導的方式,帶你走過整個流程。

emails.subject: 3 ways to bounce back after breaking your habit streak
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Forming new habits is tough.

Whenever we adopt a new habit, we must train ourselves to do something that runs counter to our current routines. These routines can be so deeply ingrained that they seem impossible to break.

I'll bet you can relate. See if the following scenarios sound familiar.

* You commit to eating healthy. After doing so successfully for a week, you stumble upon your favorite junk food. You're unable to resist, and there goes your diet.

* You commit to writing in a journal each morning. After a month, you inadvertently skip a day. You don't mean to do so. You just forget, and there goes your month-long streak.

* You tell yourself that you're going to visit the gym each afternoon after you get home from work. And you do so for a few weeks. Then, one day, you arrive home feeling exhausted. It was a particularly stressful day at your job, and you want nothing more than to relax with a glass of wine and Netflix. There goes your gym routine.

All of us go through this when we adopt new habits. We stumble. We make mistakes. It's a natural part of the process.

It doesn't matter how important the habits are. They might completely transform our lives. Yet we still manage to slip up.

Frustrating, right?

When this happens, don't beat yourself up about it. Don't think of these misfires as failures. Think of them as minor hiccups.

Here are three things you can do to quickly get back on track. They've worked for me, and I'll bet they'll work for you, too.

#1 - Take a small step back

One of the keys to adopting any new habit is to take micro steps. Start small and build slowly.

For example, suppose you want to jog for 45 minutes each morning. Start by jogging for 5 minutes for a few days. Then, jog for 10 minutes over the next few days. Then, do it for 15 minutes the following week. And so on.

Now, let's say you miss a few days. No problem. Take a step back. For example, if you've been jogging for 30 minutes a day and slip up, commit to jogging for just 20 minutes tomorrow. Or even 10 minutes.

Making a smaller commitment will help get you back in the saddle.

#2 - Put the habit on your daily schedule

Make it an appointment with yourself.

For example, let's say you're committed to practicing the guitar each day. But your life gets busy, and you abandon the habit.

Get back on track by putting your daily practice session on your schedule. Don't just put it on your to-do list. Actually block off time on your daily calendar.

Treat it like an important, can't-miss appointment.

#3 - Commit to doing just a tiny bit

It's funny how the brain works. We pride ourselves on being rational, reasonable, and logical, but we can actually trick our brains into doing something it doesn't want to do.

This can be very useful when we're trying to form new habits and need to get back on track after screwing up.

Tell yourself that you'll do just a tiny bit.

For example, suppose you're committed to working out for 45 minutes a day. You have an entire workout regimen. But for whatever reason, you skip a day. You just don't feel like working out. Then, you skip another day. And another.

After skipping workouts for an entire week, getting back on track may seem impossible.

Try this: tell yourself that you'll just do five pushups. Forget your carefully-planned regimen. Just focus on doing five pushups.

Once you start, your mind will want to continue. That's what I mean by "tricking your brain." It's like persuading your child to try a new food you're certain he'll love. Focus on getting him to take the first bite.

Adopting new habits is rarely easy. Often we have to change years of mental programming before we can accept the new routines. Missteps are inevitable.

The good news is, you can easily bounce back if you slip up. Try the three "tricks" above. You may be surprised by how effective they are.

I've bent your ear long enough today. My next email will be much shorter. I promise. :)

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you're struggling to form new habits, my book Small Habits Revolution can help. It describes, in step-by-step detail, how to adopt new habits and make them stick.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

養成新習慣是件苦差事。

每當我們想採納一個新習慣,就必須訓練自己做一些與目前routine背道而馳的事。而這些routine往往根深蒂固,幾乎讓人覺得難以打破。

我敢說你一定有同感。看看下面這些情境是不是很熟悉。

* 你決心要健康飲食。成功執行一週後,你不小心遇到了你最愛的垃圾食物。你抵擋不住誘惑,於是你的飲食計畫就這樣泡湯了。

* 你決心每天早上寫日記。一個月後,你不小心漏掉了一天。你並非故意,只是忘記了,於是維持了一個月的連續紀錄就這樣中斷了。

* 你告訴自己下班回家後每天下午都要去健身房。你確實做到了好幾週。然後有一天,你拖著疲憊的身軀回到家。那天工作特別累人,你只想來杯紅酒配Netflix放鬆一下。於是你的健身routine就這樣被打斷了。

每個人在採納新習慣時都會經歷這些。我們會跌跌撞撞,會犯錯。這是整個過程中很自然的一部分。

無論這些習慣有多重要——即使它們可能徹底改變我們的人生——我們仍然難免會失手。

很令人沮喪,對吧?

當這種情況發生時,別苛責自己。別把這些失誤當作失敗,把它們當成小小的顛簸就好。

以下是三件能幫你快速重回正軌的事。它們對我很有效,我敢說對你也一樣管用。

#1 - 稍微退後一步

養成任何新習慣的關鍵之一,就是採取「微小步驟」。從小處著手,慢慢累積。

舉例來說,假設你想每天早上慢跑45分鐘。可以先從連續幾天慢跑5分鐘開始。接下來幾天慢跑10分鐘。再下一週做到15分鐘,依此類推。

現在,假設你漏了幾天。沒關係,退後一步就好。舉例來說,如果你原本每天慢跑30分鐘卻失手了,那就承諾明天只慢跑20分鐘,甚至10分鐘也行。

訂下較小的承諾,能幫助你重新回到軌道上。

#2 - 把這個習慣排進你的每日行程

把它當作與自己的一個約定。

舉例來說,假設你決心每天練習吉他,但生活變得忙碌,於是你放棄了這個習慣。

把每日練習時段排進你的行事曆中,藉此重回正軌。不要只是把它列在待辦清單上,而是要在每日行事曆上真正劃出時間。

把它當作一個重要、不可錯過的約會來對待。

#3 - 承諾只做一點點就好

大腦的運作方式很有趣。我們自豪於自己是理性、講道理、有邏輯的,但實際上我們可以「欺騙」自己的大腦去做它原本不想做的事。

當我們想養成新習慣,並在搞砸後需要重回正軌時,這一招特別有用。

告訴自己,你只需要做一點點就好。

舉例來說,假設你決心每天運動45分鐘,你有一整套完整的健身計畫。但不知為何,你跳過了一天,就是提不起勁運動。接著你又跳過了一天,再一天。

整整跳過一週的運動後,重回正軌似乎變得遙不可及。

試試這個方法:告訴自己只要做五下伏地挺身就好。忘掉你精心規劃的整套計畫,只專注在完成五下伏地挺身。

一旦你開始了,你的心智就會想繼續下去。這就是我所謂的「欺騙大腦」。這就像哄你的孩子嘗試一種你確信他會喜歡的新食物——重點是先讓他咬下第一口。

養成新習慣很少是件容易的事。我們通常必須改變多年來的心智慣性,才能接受新的routine。失誤在所難免。

好消息是,一旦失手,你也能輕鬆地重回正軌。試試上面這三個「小訣竅」,你可能會驚訝於它們有多有效。

今天已經佔用你不少時間了。我保證下一封信會短很多。:)

咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你正為養成新習慣所苦,我的書《Small Habits Revolution》能幫上忙。書中以逐步詳盡的方式,說明如何採納新習慣並讓它們持續下去。

emails.subject: 5 personality traits that increase the odds you'll procrastinate
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

If you struggle with procrastination, you're not alone. Putting off until tomorrow that which we can do today is human nature.

In fact, evidence suggests that procrastination is linked to our personalities. Certain traits make us more likely to stall and postpone things.

Today, we'll cover five such traits. I can tell you from personal experience they definitely contribute to a tendency to procrastinate.

#1 - The Constant Worrier

If you're always worried about catastrophes looming around the corner, it'll be difficult to take action. You'll be anxious that your actions might cause a catastrophe.

Naturally, you'll be tempted to wait until circumstances seem safer and more certain.

#2 - The Incessant Perfectionist

If getting every detail right and making zero mistakes is a priority to you, you're going to put off tasks and projects.

Sometimes, it'll be a matter of poor time management. You'll spend an inordinate amount of time perfecting something, ignoring everything else in the process. Other times, it's be due to anxiety and unrealistic expectations. You'll be unable to act because you'll be afraid that whatever you do won't be good enough.

I dealt this beast for many years. If you're a perfectionist, I know what you're going through.

#3 - The Perpetual Idealist

It's okay to daydream. Indulging in fantasies about things we want to achieve is harmless...

... as long as the daydreams are short-lived.

The problem comes when we dwell on the ideal and never manage to create a detailed action plan. Without a plan in place, we end up postponing things, telling ourselves "someday."

#4 - The Self-Perceived Imposter

Despite your past accomplishments, you may feel inadequate to tackle the task in front of you. Perhaps you feel you deserve neither the responsibility nor others' confidence.

This is called "imposter syndrome." You chalk up your past successes as owing to luck rather than your skills. And because you can't rely on luck, you have trouble getting started.

#5 - The Overwhelmed

When you're drowning under a flood of responsibilities, expectations, and emotions, it seems impossible to take action. It feels like there's too much on your plate.

Making matters worse, your inner critic gets into the act, telling you that you're feeling overwhelmed because you're not good enough to handle everything.

So you procrastinate.

I won't bore you with my personal horror stories about this stuff. Suffice to say, if you deal with any of the above, I relate and empathize.

The good news is, you can train yourself to take action when you feel like stalling. It doesn't require purging the above personality traits. Rather, it's a matter of being aware of them and refusing to let them control you.

I have some ideas to share on the matter, but this email is already long enough.

We'll revisit this in the near future.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you're tired of procrastinating and want to break the habit, you may find my book The Procrastination Cure helpful. It's filled with the tactics I used to train myself to stop putting things off. I'll bet many of them will work for you, too.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

如果你有拖延的問題,你並不孤單。把今天能做的事延到明天,是人類的天性。

事實上,有證據顯示拖延與我們的人格特質有關。某些特質會讓我們更容易拖延、延後事情。

今天,我們就來談談五種這樣的特質。以我個人經驗來說,我可以告訴你,它們確實會助長拖延的傾向。

#1 - 「時刻擔憂型」

如果你總是擔心災難即將降臨,那麼採取行動就會變得困難。你會擔心自己的行動可能會招致災難。

自然而然地,你會傾向等到情況看起來更安全、更確定時再行動。

#2 - 「無止盡的完美主義型」

如果把每個細節做到完美、零失誤視為優先要務,你就會不斷拖延任務與專案。

有時候,這是時間管理不佳的問題——你會花費過多時間去完善某件事,而在這過程中忽略了其他一切。有時候,則是源於焦慮與不切實際的期待——你會因為害怕自己做的事不夠好,而遲遲無法行動。

我曾與這頭「猛獸」纏鬥多年。如果你是完美主義者,我完全懂你正在經歷什麼。

#3 - 「永恆的理想主義型」

做白日夢並無不可。沉浸在對想達成之事的幻想中是無害的……

……只要這些白日夢是短暫的。

問題出在,當我們一直沉溺於理想,卻始終無法制定出具體的行動計畫時。沒有計畫,我們最終只會一再拖延,告訴自己「總有一天」。

#4 - 「自認冒牌者型」

儘管你過去有所成就,你可能仍覺得自己不足以應付眼前的任務。也許你覺得自己不配擁有這份責任,也不配得到他人的信任。

這叫做「冒牌者症候群」。你把過去的成功歸功於運氣,而非自己的能力。而由於你無法「依賴」運氣,你就很難開始行動。

#5 - 「不堪重負型」

當你被排山倒海的責任、期待與情緒淹沒時,採取行動似乎變得不可能。你會感覺自己肩上的擔子太多太重。

更糟的是,你內心的批評者這時也跳出來插一腳,告訴你之所以感到不堪重負,是因為你不夠好,無法應付這一切。

於是你就拖延了。

我就不用自己的親身慘痛經歷來煩你了。總之,如果你也面臨上述任何一種情況,我完全能感同身受。

好消息是,即使你想拖延,你也能訓練自己採取行動。這並不需要根除上述的人格特質,而是需要覺察它們,並拒絕讓它們主宰你。

關於這個主題我還有些想法想分享,但這封信已經夠長了。

我們近期會再回頭談這個話題。

咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你厭倦了拖延,想要戒掉這個習慣,你可能會覺得我的書《The Procrastination Cure》很有幫助。書中充滿了我用來訓練自己停止拖延的各種戰術。我敢說其中許多也會對你有效。

emails.subject: Here's how to prioritize when you're overwhelmed by your to-do list
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Ever had one of those days when your to-do list is a mile long and there's just not enough time to do everything?

Making matters worse, people keep demanding your attention and asking for your help.

Yeah, we've all had those days. Frustrating, right?

That's when it becomes critical to prioritize tasks. If we don't, we risk getting buried under a mountain of to-do items, some of which aren't even important to us.

Today, I'm going to share a method for separating the stuff you must get done from the stuff that only seems consequential.

It's not my method. It springs from something former U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower said back in the 50s.

He said, "I have two kinds of problems: the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent."

That became known as the Eisenhower Principle. And it's a terrific way to manage your workload, whether you're at home or in the office.

Here's how it works...

URGENT describes things that need your attention right now.

IMPORTANT describes things that'll help you to achieve a desired outcome.

With that in mind, create the following four lists:

1. Important and urgent

2. Important but not urgent

3. Not important but urgent

4. Not important and not urgent

Next, assign every to-do item to one of these four lists.

List #1 is reserved for tasks that not only demand your immediate attention, but will also help you to reach your goals. If you're a student, this might mean finishing an assignment on deadline. If you work from home, it could include finishing a project for a client.

List #2 is where you'll put tasks that'll help you to achieve your goals, but don't require your attention at this moment. Examples include exercising, meditating, or planning a date night for you and your spouse.

List #3 is for tasks that demand your immediate attention, but contribute nothing toward your goals. At the office, this might include random phone calls or coworkers who stop by to chat. At home, this could include a friend or family member who stops by unannounced.

List #4 is for distractions. It's for the stuff you WANT to do that won't contribute to any desired outcome. Stuff that's neither urgent nor important. This is where you'll put things like binge-watching Grey's Anatomy or The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, playing Fortnight or Minecraft, or catching up on Instagram.

You've done the hard part. Now, it's just a matter of focusing your attention.

Spend the majority of your time and energy completing tasks found on List #1 and List #2. That's where you'll have the greatest impact. If you have time left over, address the stuff on the other two lists.

And if you don't have time (or energy) for them, don't be afraid to let them go. After all, they're not going to help you to reach your goals.

Let's Sum It Up

Some tasks are important. Some are urgent. Some are both. And some are neither.

Allocating your time accordingly will prevent you from getting overwhelmed when you have more demands on your time than time itself.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. A lot of folks create to-do lists without a clear strategy. Important tasks fall through the cracks, which gets intensely frustrating over time. If you're struggling with this common issue, I encourage you to check out my book To-Do List Formula.

嗨 張振輝,

你是否有過這樣的日子:待辦清單長得沒完沒了,時間卻怎麼也不夠用?

更糟的是,還有人不斷要求你的注意力,請你幫忙。

是啊,我們都經歷過這種日子。很令人沮喪,對吧?

這時候,「排定任務優先順序」就變得至關重要。如果不這麼做,我們就有可能被堆積如山的待辦事項淹沒,而其中有些甚至根本不重要。

今天,我要跟你分享一個方法,用來區分「必須完成的事」與「只是看起來很重要的事」。

這不是我發明的方法。它源自美國前總統艾森豪(Dwight D. Eisenhower)在1950年代說過的一句話。

他說:「我有兩種問題:緊急的與重要的。緊急的事通常不重要,重要的事則從來不緊急。」

這後來被稱為「艾森豪原則」。無論是在家裡還是在辦公室,這都是管理工作量的絕佳方法。

運作方式是這樣的……

「緊急」指的是需要你立刻處理的事。

「重要」指的是有助於你達成期望結果的事。

有了這個概念後,建立以下四個清單:

1. 重要且緊急

2. 重要但不緊急

3. 不重要但緊急

4. 不重要也不緊急

接著,把每一項待辦事項分配到這四個清單中的其中一個。

清單一保留給那些不僅需要你立即處理、也有助於你達成目標的任務。如果你是學生,這可能表示要準時完成一份作業;如果你在家工作,則可能包括為客戶完成一項專案。

清單二則放那些有助於達成目標、但當下不需要你立刻處理的任務。例如運動、冥想,或為你和伴侶規劃一個約會之夜。

清單三放那些需要你立即處理、但對你的目標毫無幫助的任務。在辦公室,這可能包括突如其來的電話,或是同事跑來閒聊;在家中,這可能包括未事先告知就來訪的朋友或家人。

清單四是給干擾事項用的。這是那些你「想」做、但對任何期望結果都沒有貢獻的事——既不緊急也不重要的事。像是一口氣追完《實習醫生》或《漫才梅索太太》、玩《Fortnite》或《Minecraft》,或是滑Instagram。

困難的部分你已經做完了。現在,只剩下把注意力集中起來而已。

把大部分的時間與精力,花在完成清單一與清單二上的任務。那裡才是你能發揮最大影響力的地方。如果還有剩餘時間,再處理另外兩個清單上的事。

如果你沒有時間(或精力)處理它們,也不用害怕放手。畢竟,它們並不會幫助你達成目標。

總結一下

有些任務重要,有些緊急,有些兩者兼具,有些兩者皆非。

依此分配你的時間,能讓你在時間需求超過時間本身時,不至於被壓垮。

咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 很多人在建立待辦清單時,都沒有清楚的策略。重要任務因此被漏掉,久而久之會讓人非常沮喪。如果你也為這個常見問題所苦,我鼓勵你看看我的書《To-Do List Formula》。

emails.subject: 3 simple (and unorthodox) hacks to improve your focus
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

The last few emails I've sent you have been pretty long. So, let's keep this one short.

Today, I'm going to share with you 3 unconventional tips that'll improve your focus and help you to fight distractions. By "unconventional" I mean they're outside the normal fare.

Each one is simple and easy to practice. That means you can use them starting today.

Enough blather. Let's jump right in.

Unconventional Tip #1 - Work on Something Entirely Different

When you can't concentrate, give yourself something to do that's a total departure from whatever you're working on.

For example, let's say you're working on a boring spreadsheet, and your mind keeps wandering. Get some paper and start journaling for a few minutes. Or create song lyrics. Or come up with a witty haiku.

Or let's say you're writing a novel, and you keep getting distracted. Grab some paper and do a few math problems. For example, multiply 32,537 and 64,319.

Sound silly? Don't dismiss it. You may find that it stimulates your brain in a way that lets you get back to the task at hand with renewed focus.

Unconventional Tip #2 - Take a Break

When we get distracted, it's tempting to fight through the distraction. We tell ourselves, "C'mon. Get it together. Stop being such a ninny. FOCUS!"

We get frustrated with ourselves, which, ironically, makes us more distracted. That, in turn, amps up our frustration.

It's a terrible cycle.

What we should do is take a break.

When you're unable to concentrate, stop what you're doing. Stand up (if you're sitting). Walk away. Get a glass of water. Take a 10-minute walk outside. Get some fresh air.

You'll be surprised at how well it clears the mind.

Unconventional Tip #3 - Clear Your Workspace

My office used to be a pigsty. Dirt and grime weren't the problems. Paper was. Snail mail, stuff I printed from my computer, countless files, etc.

The clutter destroyed my ability to focus. Everything distracted me.

Can you guess what happened when I cleared my workspace? Suddenly, I could manage the distractions. I was finally able to concentrate.

I have a lot more unorthodox hacks for improving your focus. But let's stop here for today. I wanted to keep this email short and it's already getting a bit too long.

Try the above tips. And let me know if they help!

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you're having trouble concentrating, you're not alone. Everyone deals with this problem. You may find my book Fast Focus to be the solution you need. In it, I describe the tactics that worked for me.

emails.subject: How to take criticism like a pro (without feeling like a failure)
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I used to hate criticism.

Whenever someone pointed out something I had done wrong, I'd get defensive. I'd argue. I'd become suspicious of their motivations.

And I'm ashamed to admit, I'd find something I found lacking in THEM and go on the offensive. I'd attack.

To say I lacked grace when confronted with criticism is the understatement of a lifetime.

I wanted everyone to think everything I did was perfect. So disapproval was a personal attack on me.

At least, that was my perspective back then. I'm not proud of it.

I've since let go of my inner perfectionist. I've learned to not only accept constructive criticism, but look forward to it.

And it has made a HUGE difference in my life. It has improved the way I communicate. It has helped me to refine how I write books. It has allowed me to handle problems with less frustration and more insight.

Let's say you're in the same boat I was. Let's suppose you loathe constructive criticism. You know deep inside that you should be open to it. But it's hard to get there.

Here are a few tips that worked for me...

1. Don't react.

I know, it's instinctive. But try to suppress the instinct. Try not to furrow your brow or scrunch up your face. And don't be like me in years past, responding "Yeah? Well, you're terrible, also!"

2. Ask yourself, "Will this feedback help me?"

Chances are, the criticism highlights something you can improve. If so, you can benefit by taking it to heart. Why not take advantage of it?

3. Recognize that the person giving feedback isn't trying to tear you down.

People who are kind enough to offer constructive feedback truly want to help you.

Oh sure, we've all dealt with people who "offer feedback" as a weapon. But in my experience, they're in the minority. And hopefully you're avoiding such people because they're a bummer to hang around.

MOST folks are eager to help.

4. Ask questions to clarify the feedback.

Constructive criticism usually starts out bland. The person giving it doesn't want to offend you. To get to the juicy details, the stuff that's really helpful, you need to ask questions.

For example, suppose a friend says, "I've noticed you're often distracted when we talk." You might ask, "Can you tell me the last time you noticed that?"

The circumstances surrounding your distraction might reveal why it's happening and how you can stop it.

That's it for now.

Let's talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you struggle with perfectionism, I can definitely relate. You may find my book The Joy of Imperfection helpful, especially when it comes to taking constructive criticism.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

我以前很討厭被批評。

每當有人指出我做錯的地方,我就會變得防衛心很重。我會爭辯,會開始懷疑對方的動機。

而且我很慚愧地承認,我還會反過來挑出對方的缺點,展開反擊。我會攻擊對方。

說我在面對批評時缺乏氣度,實在是這輩子最輕描淡寫的說法了。

我希望每個人都認為我做的每件事都完美無缺,所以任何不認同對我而言都是人身攻擊。

至少,那是我當時的想法。我對此並不引以為傲。

後來,我逐漸放下了心中的完美主義。我學會不僅接受建設性的批評,甚至還開始期待它。

這為我的人生帶來了「巨大」的改變。它改善了我溝通的方式,幫助我精進寫書的方式,也讓我能以更少的挫折感、更多的洞察力去處理問題。

假設你和我當年一樣,厭惡建設性批評。你內心深處知道自己應該對此保持開放,但很難真正做到。

以下是幾個對我有效的訣竅……

1. 別立刻反應。

我知道,這是本能反應。但試著壓下這個本能。試著別皺眉、別擺臭臉。也別像我當年那樣,回嘴說:「是喔?那你也很爛啊!」

2. 問問自己:「這個回饋對我有幫助嗎?」

很有可能,這個批評指出了你可以改進的地方。如果是這樣,把它放在心上對你會有益處。為什麼不好好利用它呢?

3. 認清給你回饋的人並非想要打擊你。

願意善意提供建設性回饋的人,是真心想幫助你的。

當然,我們都遇過把「提供回饋」當作武器的人。但依我的經驗,這樣的人是少數。希望你也懂得避開這類讓人相處起來很掃興的人。

「大多數」人其實都是樂於幫忙的。

4. 提出問題,釐清回饋的內容。

建設性批評通常一開始都說得很含糊。提出批評的人不想冒犯你。要挖出真正有價值、有幫助的細節,你需要主動發問。

舉例來說,假設一位朋友說:「我注意到我們聊天時你常常分心。」你可以問:「你可以告訴我,你最近一次注意到是什麼時候嗎?」

那些造成你分心的具體情境,或許能揭露出原因,以及你該如何停止這種情況。

emails.subject: 5 simple things ultra-productive people do every day
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Everything I know about productivity comes from other people.

I watch them. I talk to them. When it comes to famous folks like Richard Branson, Elon Musk, or the late Steve Jobs, I read their interviews.

And then I model them. That's the most important bit. I apply their productivity hacks to my life.

Some of their tips work for me. Some don't. I keep the former and chuck the latter.

And little by little, I find ways to get more done in less time. Then, I share the good stuff with you so we can grow together.

With that in mind, let's take a quick look at five things highly-productive people do each day.

A couple may surprise you. I encourage you to put them to the test.

#1 - Work when you're most productive.

I'm a morning person. I get up at 5:00 a.m. After I go through my morning routine, I get right to work.

But that's just me. You may be at your most productive in the afternoon. Or in the evening. Work according to your energy levels.

#2 - Carry a notepad.

Or a stack of index cards. Or a note-taking app on your phone. It doesn't matter what you use.

The important thing is that you can jot down thoughts as they occur to you. Get them out of your head so you can focus. Then, revisit them later.

#3 - Break up your day into time chunks.

Your calendar probably has tiny holes. These holes represent idle time.

For example, suppose you block off an hour on your calendar for a meeting you expect to last 40 minutes.

What do you do with the remaining 20 minutes? If you haven't scheduled anything, they probably slip through your fingers. I know this because that's exactly what happens to me.

Use time chunks. Don't think of your day in terms of HOURS. Think in terms of MINUTES.

Forty minutes for a meeting. Twenty minutes to check email. Ninety minutes to work on a report that's due next week. And so on.

#4 - Limit the amount of time you spend on each task.

This tip complements tip #3.

Don't just put things on a to-do list and hope for the best. Assign each task a specific amount of time.

For example, got a meeting today that'll take 40 minutes? Write down "40 min" next to it on your to-do list. Need to work on a report for 90 minutes? Write down "90 min" next to it.

Don't allow yourself to exceed the time you set aside. Remember Parkinson's law: "work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion."

#5 - Say "no" more often.

This tip is dear to me. It changed my life for the better.

We're naturally inclined to say yes to requests. We want to be helpful. We want to be supportive.

The problem is, most of us have a difficult time balancing our own obligations with others' obligations. In our haste to help others, we neglect the stuff that's on OUR plates.

Say "no" more often. You'll be less distracted, more focused, and have more time to accomplish whatever you need to get done.

See a tip that you're not currently using? If so, try it out for yourself.

If you notice a boost in your productivity, terrific! If you don't, move on to the next one. Remember, becoming more productive is ultimately about testing things and finding what works best for you.

Everything else is just noise.

That's it for today.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you'd like to be more productive, but aren't sure where to start, check out my book The 30-Day Productivity Plan. It's a step-by-step blueprint.

嗨 張振輝,

我對生產力的所有了解都來自其他人。

我觀察他們,和他們交談。至於像理查·布蘭森(Richard Branson)、伊隆·馬斯克(Elon Musk),或已故的史蒂夫·賈伯斯(Steve Jobs)這樣的知名人物,我則會閱讀他們的訪談。

然後,我會「模仿」他們——這是最重要的一步。我把他們的生產力技巧套用到自己的生活中。

他們的一些訣竅對我有效,有些則沒有。我保留有效的,丟掉沒用的。

然後,一點一滴地,我找到了在更短時間內完成更多事情的方法。接著,我把這些好東西分享給你,讓我們一起成長。

有了這個想法,我們就來快速看看高生產力人士每天會做的五件事。

有幾件可能會讓你感到意外。我鼓勵你親自試試看。

#1 - 在你生產力最高的時段工作。

我是個晨型人。我早上5點起床,做完晨間例行公事後,就直接開始工作。

但這只是我的情況。你的生產力高峰可能在下午,或是晚上。依照你自己的精力狀態來安排工作。

#2 - 隨身攜帶筆記本。

或是一疊索引卡,或是手機上的筆記App,用什麼都沒關係。

重要的是,當靈感浮現時,你能立刻寫下來。把它們從腦中卸下,好讓你能專注,之後再回頭查看。

#3 - 把一天切割成時間區塊。

你的行事曆可能有許多小小的空隙,這些空隙代表著閒置的時間。

舉例來說,假設你在行事曆上劃出一小時開會,但預期會議只需要40分鐘。

剩下的20分鐘你要拿來做什麼?如果你沒有預先安排任何事,這些時間很可能就這樣悄悄溜走了。我很清楚這一點,因為我自己就是這樣。

使用時間區塊。別用「小時」來思考你的一天,而要用「分鐘」來思考。

開會40分鐘、查看電子郵件20分鐘、處理下週要交的報告90分鐘,依此類推。

#4 - 限制花在每項任務上的時間。

這個訣竅是第3點的延伸。

不要只是把事情列在待辦清單上,然後盼望一切順利。為每項任務分配一段具體的時間。

舉例來說,今天有場會議要開40分鐘?就在待辦清單上那項旁邊寫下「40分鐘」。需要花90分鐘處理一份報告?就寫下「90分鐘」。

別讓自己超出預留的時間。記住帕金森定律:「工作會不斷擴張,以填滿完成它所可用的時間。」

#5 - 更常說「不」。

這個訣竅對我而言意義重大,它徹底改善了我的人生。

我們天生傾向對請求說「好」。我們想幫上忙,想展現支持。

問題是,大多數人都很難在自己的責任與他人的責任之間取得平衡。在急於幫助他人的過程中,我們反而忽略了「自己」份內的事。

更常說「不」吧。你會更少分心、更專注,也會有更多時間完成你需要完成的事。

看到一個你目前還沒使用的訣竅了嗎?如果有,那就親自試試看吧。

如果你發現生產力有所提升,太好了!如果沒有,那就試試下一個。記住,提升生產力終究是不斷嘗試,並找出最適合「你」的方法的過程。

其他一切都只是雜音。

今天就講到這裡。

咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你想提升生產力,卻不知從何開始,可以看看我的書《The 30-Day Productivity Plan》,這是一份逐步引導的藍圖。

emails.subject: How to make better decisions by predicting your future regret
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Whenever we make hard decisions, we typically think about the various courses of action available to us and then envision their respective outcomes.

What will happen if we choose option A? What might happen if we select option B? How about option C?

And so forth.

Then, we'll usually go with the option that gets us closest to our desired result.

But what if there's a better way to make decisions? One that allows us to minimize our efforts and still feel wholly satisfied - and even delighted - with our results?

I'm happy to report there is such a way.

It involves imagining your future regret and using it as a predictive signal in your decision-making. By doing so, you can quickly let go of a lot of unnecessary pursuits and use that saved time and energy toward activities that'll make you happier.

Here's an example...

Let's say you're contemplating writing a novel. You estimate it'll take 12 months of diligent, butt-in-chair action to complete.

That's a lot of time to sacrifice. Moreover, it's not an easy job. Writing a novel is hard, and often frustrating, work.

So, should you do it?

Suppose your desired result is to become an author. You might be tempted to make your decision based solely on that aspiration.

But try this...

Ask yourself, "How much would I regret never having written this novel?"

If the answer is, "Not much," then you can confidently dismiss your plan to do so. And you can spend the time and effort you would've devoted to that monumental task on pursuits that are likelier to make you happy.

Sometimes, your answer will be, "Yeah, I'll definitely regret not moving forward on this plan."

That's when you know it's important to take action.

Jeff Bezos once explained his motivation to create Amazon. He said he wouldn't have regretted failing, but he sure would've regretted having never tried. What's worse, he claims that regret would've haunted him every day of his life.

So, he made what he calls "an incredibly easy decision" and created Amazon.

If you're struggling with an important decision, envision your future regret for every potential outcome. You may find doing so is the easiest way to choose the best option and avoid a lot of unnecessary stress and effort in the process.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. Using future regret to make better decisions aligns perfectly with the 80/20 rule. If you'd like to use this rule to simplify your life, check out my book 80/20 Your Life!
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

每當我們要做出艱難的決定時,通常會思考各種可行的行動方案,然後想像各自可能帶來的結果。

如果選擇方案A會發生什麼事?選擇方案B又可能發生什麼事?那方案C呢?

依此類推。

然後,我們通常會選擇最能讓我們接近期望結果的那個方案。

但如果有一種更好的決策方式呢?一種能讓我們把力氣降到最低,結果卻依然讓我們感到十分滿意——甚至喜出望外的方式?

我很高興地告訴你,確實有這樣一種方法。

這個方法是:想像你未來可能產生的遺憾,並把它當作決策時的預測訊號。這麼做,你就能迅速放下許多不必要的追求,把省下來的時間與精力,投注在更可能讓你快樂的事情上。

舉個例子……

假設你正在考慮寫一本小說,你估計需要12個月勤奮不懈、腳踏實地的努力才能完成。

這是一段不小的時間犧牲,而且這也不是件容易的工作。寫小說是件辛苦、而且常常令人挫折的差事。

那麼,你該不該去做呢?

假設你想要的結果是成為一名作家,你可能會單純基於這個渴望來做決定。

但不妨試試這個方法……

問問自己:「如果我從未寫出這本小說,我會有多後悔?」

如果答案是「不會太後悔」,那你就可以放心地放棄這個計畫,把原本要投入這項艱鉅任務的時間與精力,轉而用在更可能帶給你快樂的追求上。

有時候,你的答案會是:「會,如果我沒有推進這個計畫,我一定會後悔。」

那時你就知道,採取行動是很重要的。

傑夫·貝佐斯(Jeff Bezos)曾解釋他創立亞馬遜的動機。他說,即使失敗了他也不會後悔,但如果從未嘗試過,他一定會後悔。更糟的是,他說那樣的遺憾會纏繞他一輩子,天天如此。

於是,他做出了他所謂「一個非常容易的決定」,創立了亞馬遜。

如果你正為一個重要的決定所苦,不妨想像每個可能結果所帶來的未來遺憾。你可能會發現,這是選出最佳方案、並在過程中避免許多不必要壓力與心力耗損的最簡單方法。

咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 運用未來的遺憾來做出更好的決定,與80/20法則完美契合。如果你想運用這個法則來簡化你的生活,可以看看我的書《80/20 Your Life!》。

emails.subject: 7 bad things that happen when you're too nice (and how to avoid them)
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

It's natural to want to do things for other people. It feels good and it's helpful. Everyone wins, right?

Not so fast.

There are lots of downsides to being too nice. You may not notice them at first, but they creep up on you. Over time, they can make you feel resentful, exhausted, and unappreciated.

That's no way to live.

With that in mind, let's take a quick look at seven ways being too nice negatively impacts you. Then, I'll show you how to fix the problem.

#1 - The more you give, the more people will expect you to give.

Giving of yourself isn't bad, of course. But it's easy to fall into the trap of giving so much that you forget to address your own needs.

#2 - Needy people will swarm you.

Word travels fast when you repeatedly volunteer to help others. Eventually, you become the first person they ask for help.

#3 - Many will take advantage of your continual kindness.

Some folks are manipulative. When they discover that you haven't set boundaries, they'll try to take advantage of you.

#4 - Others may see you as weak.

When you say yes to every request and repeatedly set aside your needs to help others, some people will think of you as weak. That perception can make it difficult for others to take you seriously.

#5 - Some people will distrust you.

It sounds crazy, but it's true. Some folks are instinctively suspicious of people who are nice by nature. They assume everyone has an ulterior motive.

#6 - You'll set yourself up for disappointment.

When you constantly give of yourself to others, it's natural to expect them to reciprocate when you need help. But those expectations may be unrealistic.

#7 - You'll forget to address your own needs.

Helping others feels deeply rewarding (hello oxytocin!). The problem is, when you spend all of your time helping people, there isn't much time to take care of your needs. If this goes on long enough, you'll eventually feel depressed, bitter, and exhausted.

So how can we fix this problem? How can we stop being too nice?

The answer is simple. It's the execution that causes some folks to stumble.

The solution is to start saying no. Of course, if you're a longtime people-pleaser, it's easier said than done. You may be trying to reverse years of programming.

Try this:

First, recognize that you deserve better treatment. Your needs are as valid as others' needs.

Second, acknowledge that your time is valuable and limited.

Third, write down your commitments. Think of the time and attention you owe your family, your spouse, your friends, and your boss. And of course, don't forget about yourself!

Fourth, practice saying no. You don't have to rebuff everyone who comes to you for help. Say no just once today. Then, do it again tomorrow. The day after, say it two times. Practice makes perfect. And taking baby steps makes it easier.

Fifth, don't apologize for being unavailable to help. That only reinforces the idea that you're doing something wrong.

That's enough for today. I hope something above strikes a chord with you. I can confidently say that if you're a people-pleaser, learning to say no will improve your life.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you're having difficulty turning people down when they ask for help, check out my book The Art of Saying NO. It's filled with actionable advice.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

想為別人做點事是很自然的。這感覺很好,也很有幫助。大家都能受益,對吧?

先別急著這麼想。

過度友善其實有許多壞處。你可能一開始不會察覺,但它們會悄悄找上你。久而久之,可能讓你感到憤懣、疲憊,且不被珍惜。

那不是一種好的生活方式。

有鑑於此,我們先快速看看「過度友善」對你造成負面影響的七種方式。接著,我會告訴你如何解決這個問題。

#1 - 你給得越多,別人就會期待你給得更多。

付出自己當然不是壞事。但很容易陷入一個陷阱:給得太多,以致忘了照顧自己的需求。

#2 - 需索無度的人會蜂擁而至。

當你一再自願幫助別人,消息很快就會傳開。最終,你會成為他們第一個尋求幫助的對象。

#3 - 許多人會利用你持續不斷的善意。

有些人善於操控他人。當他們發現你沒有設下界線,就會試圖利用你。

#4 - 有些人可能會認為你軟弱。

當你對每個請求都說好,並一再為了幫助別人而擱置自己的需求時,有些人會認為你軟弱。這種印象會讓別人難以認真看待你。

#5 - 有些人反而會不信任你。

聽起來很瘋狂,但這是真的。有些人會本能地對天性善良的人抱持懷疑,他們會假設每個人都有不可告人的動機。

#6 - 你會為自己種下失望的種子。

當你不斷付出自己給別人時,很自然會期待在你需要幫助時,他們也能有所回報。但這樣的期待可能並不切實際。

#7 - 你會忘了照顧自己的需求。

幫助別人會帶來深刻的成就感(嗨,催產素!)。問題是,當你把所有時間都花在幫助別人身上,就沒有多少時間照顧自己的需求了。如果這種情況持續得夠久,你最終會感到沮喪、怨懟、疲憊不堪。

那麼,我們該如何解決這個問題?該如何停止過度友善?

答案很簡單,難的是「執行」,這才是讓有些人卡關的地方。

解決方法就是開始學會說「不」。當然,如果你長期以來都是個討好型人格,說起來容易做起來難。你可能是在試圖扭轉多年來養成的慣性。

試試這個方法:

第一,認清自己值得被更好地對待。你的需求和別人的需求一樣重要。

第二,承認自己的時間是寶貴且有限的。

第三,寫下你的各項承諾。想想你欠家人、伴侶、朋友和老闆多少時間與心力,當然,也別忘了自己!

第四,練習說「不」。你不必拒絕每一個來向你求助的人。今天就先說一次「不」,明天再說一次。後天,說兩次。熟能生巧,而從小步驟開始,能讓這件事變得更容易。

第五,不要為了無法幫忙而道歉。那只會強化「你做錯了什麼」的想法。

今天就講到這裡。希望以上內容能觸動你的某些心弦。我可以很有把握地說,如果你是個討好型人格,學會說「不」將會改善你的人生。

咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你在別人請求幫助時很難拒絕,可以看看我的書《The Art of Saying NO》,書中充滿了可實際運用的建議。

emails.subject: The first 20 minutes dictate your day...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Morning routines are important because they influence how the rest of our day will progress.

If we get up on time and complete our planned morning activities (for example, meditating or journaling), we'll feel inspired and confident as we face the day.

If we keep hitting the snooze button, finally dragging ourselves out of bed 20 minutes late, we'll end up rushing around trying to make up for lost time.

That sets a terrible tone for the rest of the day.

This is the reason we should create a simple morning routine. And ideally, it should be one that takes full advantage of our morning state of mind.

When we wake up in the morning, our brain produces alpha waves. These brainwaves keep us in a relaxed state. Research suggests they also improve our memory, increase our creativity, and help us to perform cognitive tasks.

Let's not get too far into the science of brain activity. Suffice to say these alpha waves are conducive to certain activities that can help us to get the day off to a great start.

Your morning routine will differ from mine. That's a good thing. It should be tailored to include whatever gives you the greatest sense of purpose and satisfaction.

The important thing is that you have a routine, and that you follow it every morning.

Don't currently have one? No problem. Allow me to suggest 3 simple activities. These are things that have made a real difference in my life.

#1 - Journal

Nothing fancy here. Just sit down and write whatever comes to mind. If nothing comes, doodle or draw a mind map.

There are no rules. Just let your thoughts flow.

#2 - Meditate

You don't have to sit with your legs crossed and murmur ancient chants while burning incense. Just sit in a relaxed position and let your mind wander for a couple minutes. I focus on my breathing. Maybe that'll work for you, too.

Don't worry about whether you're doing it wrong. There is no wrong.

#3 - Read

Spend a few minutes reading a personal development book. It could be about setting goals, managing your time, improving your communication, overcoming shyness, or whatever is important to you.

This puts you in a positive state of mind.

Again, you don't have to include these 3 activities in your morning routine. They're just suggestions in the event you need a few ideas.

If they work for you, fantastic. If not, chuck 'em.

Lastly, there's one thing I recommend you absolutely avoid doing when you wake up in the morning: checking your phone.

Don't fall into that rabbit hole during the first 20 minutes of your day. There'll be time for that later.

That's it for now.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you don't know where to start in creating a healthy morning routine, I suggest checking out my book Morning Makeover.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

晨間routine之所以重要,是因為它會影響一整天接下來的走向。

如果我們準時起床,並完成計畫好的晨間活動(例如冥想或寫日記),我們在面對這一天時,會感到充滿靈感與自信。

如果我們一再按下鬧鐘的延遲鍵,最後拖著身子晚了20分鐘才起床,我們就會整天匆匆忙忙,試圖彌補失去的時間。

這會為接下來的一整天定下一個很糟糕的基調。

這就是為什麼我們應該建立一個簡單的晨間routine。而理想上,這個routine應該要能充分善用我們早晨的心智狀態。

當我們早上醒來時,大腦會產生α波。這種腦波能讓我們保持放鬆的狀態。研究顯示,它們還能改善記憶力、提升創造力,並幫助我們執行認知任務。

我們就不深入探討腦部活動的科學細節了。總之,這些α波有助於某些活動,能幫助我們為一天開個好頭。

你的晨間routine會和我的不同,這是件好事。它應該量身打造,納入最能帶給你目標感與滿足感的事物。

重要的是,你「有」一套routine,而且每天早上都會遵循它。

目前還沒有嗎?沒關係。讓我提供3個簡單的活動建議,這些都是真正為我的人生帶來改變的事。

#1 - 寫日記

沒什麼花俏的,就是坐下來,寫下任何浮現腦海的東西。如果什麼都想不出來,就塗鴉或畫張心智圖。

沒有任何規則,就讓你的思緒自然流動。

#2 - 冥想

你不必盤腿而坐、燒著香、喃喃唸誦古老經文。只需以放鬆的姿勢坐著,讓心思漫遊幾分鐘。我會專注在自己的呼吸上,也許這對你也有用。

別擔心自己做得對不對,這根本沒有對錯可言。

#3 - 閱讀

花幾分鐘閱讀一本個人成長類書籍。內容可以是關於設定目標、時間管理、改善溝通、克服害羞,或任何對你而言重要的主題。

這能讓你進入一個正向的心智狀態。

再次提醒,你不必把這3項活動全都納入你的晨間routine。它們只是建議,以防你需要一些靈感。

如果它們對你有用,太好了;如果沒用,那就丟掉吧。

最後,有一件事我強烈建議你在早上起床時絕對要避免:滑手機。

別在一天的前20分鐘就掉進那個無底洞。之後有的是時間可以滑。

今天就講到這裡。

咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你不知道該從何開始建立健康的晨間routine,我建議你可以看看我的書《Morning Makeover》。

emails.subject: How lack of structure during the day impacts your happiness
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

In his book Flow, Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi notes that noon on Sunday is the "unhappiest hour in America."

Personally, I love noontime on Sundays. That's around the time that I'm getting ready to take a nap. And I really love naps.

But Csikszentmihalyi's claim piqued my curiosity. I wanted to know what he based it on.

It turns out, he interviewed thousands of people in various fields, from athletes and surgeons to artists and chess masters. From those interviews he developed a theory regarding what made people happy and what made them unhappy.

He discovered that we're happiest when we're doing exactly what we want to do. And we're unhappiest when we're doing stuff we don't care about.

Sounds obvious, right?

But it's actually insightful as it relates to how we structure our time.

According to Csikszentmihalyi, people in the U.S. tend to not structure their Sunday afternoons. It's their day off and they'd rather relax. Structure is too much like work and they don't want to think about work on Sundays.

Csikszentmihalyi says this causes people to be unfocused, unmotivated, and unproductive. And that makes them unhappy.

I don't entirely agree with this. As I mentioned, I'm completely happy at noon on Sundays because I'm getting ready to take a nap. But I'd be hard-pressed to prove that my Sunday naps were productive.

So, let me refine Csikszentmihalyi's theory based on my own experience.

I'm one of those weirdos who schedules every minute of their day. I joke with my wife that I'm the most predictable man on earth.

At 5:30 a.m., I'm working. At 9:30 a.m., I'm eating breakfast. At 12:15 p.m, I'm napping. At 1:30 p.m., I'm reading at the park. At 4:20 p.m. I'm watching something on Netflix.

And on and on, from the moment I wake up until I go to bed.

Pretty boring, right?

But I'm almost always happy. That's because I structure my days so I'm doing exactly what I want to be doing at the time I want to do it.

And that's where I think Csikszentmihalyi hits the nail on the head.

Structuring our time focuses our attention. It prevents us from spending 10 hours binge-watching something on Netflix just because it's there.

... and feeling despondent when it's over.

So here's what I'd like you to try:

Schedule your time on your next day off. Segment the entire day into time chunks, noting the precise activities you plan on doing during them.

Write down every activity, from lunch to calling your parents to watching your favorite TV show.

After the day is over, note how you feel.

You'll probably feel like it was a day well spent! Your attention was focused and you ended up doing stuff you wanted or needed to do.

And if you're like me, that'll make you pretty happy.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you're unaccustomed to using time chunks to get the most out of your day, check out my book The Time Chunking Method. It's a complete A to Z guide to the technique.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

米哈里·契克森米哈伊(Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi)在他的著作《心流》(Flow)中提到,週日中午是「美國人最不快樂的時刻」。

就我個人而言,我很喜歡週日的中午,因為那時我正準備要午睡,而我真的很愛午睡。

但契克森米哈伊的說法引起了我的好奇心,我想知道他這個結論是根據什麼得出的。

原來,他訪談了來自各行各業、成千上萬的人,從運動員、外科醫生,到藝術家、西洋棋大師都有。他從這些訪談中發展出一套關於「什麼讓人快樂、什麼讓人不快樂」的理論。

他發現,當我們正在做自己真正想做的事時,我們是最快樂的;而當我們在做自己不在乎的事時,我們是最不快樂的。

聽起來很理所當然,對吧?

但其實,這個發現在我們如何安排時間這件事上,相當具有洞見。

根據契克森米哈伊的說法,美國人往往不會為週日下午安排任何架構。那是他們的休息日,他們寧願放鬆,而「架構」讓人感覺太像工作,他們不想在週日還想著工作的事。

契克森米哈伊認為,這會導致人們變得無法專注、缺乏動力,也沒有生產力,進而讓他們感到不快樂。

我並不完全認同這個看法。如我先前所說,我在週日中午感到完全快樂,是因為我正準備要午睡。但我很難證明我的週日午睡是「有生產力的」。

所以,讓我根據自己的經驗,來修正契克森米哈伊的理論。

我是那種會把一天中每一分鐘都排好行程的怪咖。我常跟我太太開玩笑說,我是地球上最可預測的男人。

早上5:30,我在工作;早上9:30,我在吃早餐;中午12:15,我在午睡;下午1:30,我在公園看書;下午4:20,我在看Netflix。

從一起床到上床睡覺,一整天都是這樣安排。

聽起來很無聊,對吧?

但我幾乎總是很快樂。那是因為我把日子安排得井然有序,讓我在想做的時間,做著我真正想做的事。

而我認為,這正是契克森米哈伊真正說中要害的地方。

為時間建立架構,能讓我們的注意力更集中。它能防止我們只因為節目就在那裡,就花上10個小時追劇追個不停……

……然後在追完後感到心灰意冷。

所以,以下是我想請你試試看的方法:

在你下一個休假日,為自己的時間排定行程。把整天切割成一個個時間區塊,並記下你打算在每個區塊裡做的具體活動。

寫下每一項活動,從吃午餐、打電話給父母,到看你最愛的電視節目,通通寫下來。

這一天結束後,留意一下自己的感受。

你很可能會覺得這是充實的一天!你的注意力是集中的,而且你最終做的,都是你想做或需要做的事。

如果你和我一樣,那將會讓你相當快樂。

咱們再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你還不習慣用時間區塊來充分運用你的一天,可以看看我的書《The Time Chunking Method》,這是一份從A到Z、完整涵蓋這項技巧的指南。

emails.subject: Can setting goals make you feel happier?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

In 2008, an article published in the Journal of Happiness Studies made the following claim:

"The results provide preliminary support for the view that (a) goal setting and planning skills have a causal link to subjective well-being and (b) that such skills can be learned to enhance well-being."

That's fancy talk for saying that setting goals makes us feel happier.

I haven't read the actual study. It costs $40, and its conclusion is something you and I already know intuitively:

Living a carefree life might SEEM appealing to us. Who hasn't dreamed of retiring young and rich without a care in the world? But the truth is, we're happier when we have a purpose.

I know I am. Focusing on a desired outcome and planning how I'll make it happen is deeply gratifying to me.

It feels good to take these steps.

I'll bet you can relate from personal experience.

Notice that I haven't said anything about achieving the goals we set. To be sure, goal attainment makes us happy. There's no doubt about that.

But research suggests the mere act of setting goals triggers a similar emotional response.

Here's a personal example:

Recently, I sat down to plan the release of a new book I'm writing. There are a lot of moving parts. For example, I need to...

* finish writing the book
* edit it
* format it
* design the book's cover
* write the book's description for Amazon
* coordinate the audiobook's release with my narrator
* create promotional campaigns

... and I won't bore you with the rest. The point is, mapping this stuff out felt good. It made me happy to identify the destination (the book's release date) and formulate a plan for arriving there on time.

See for yourself. The next time you set goals, whether the goals are for your job, your social life, or your personal development, pay attention to how you feel. I'll bet you'll feel a sense of gratification and fulfillment.

And if you can feel this way while making plans to improve your life in some measurable way, why not take advantage of it?

That's it for today.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. Goal achievement stems from setting the right goals. If you're unsure how to do this properly, check out The P.R.I.M.E.R. Goal Setting Method.

emails.subject: How temptation bundling can help you to build new, healthy habits
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Like everyone, you have things you want to do. Things like watching your favorite TV show or indulging in your favorite dessert.

You also have things you may feel you NEED to do. Things like exercising, cooking more meals at home, and getting a decent amount of sleep each night.

So on the one hand, you have temptations. And on the other, you have healthy habits you'd like to adopt.

What if I told you that you can use the former to build the latter?

It's called temptation bundling. And it's really easy.

Here's how it works...

Think of a habit you want to develop. Let's say you want to start walking a couple miles each day.

Now, think of a favorite indulgence. For example, suppose you love the caramel macchiato at Starbucks.

We can bundle these two things.

Let's say a local Starbucks is located a mile from your home. That's perfect! Commit to walking there each afternoon and enjoying a caramel macchiato when you arrive.

Here's another example of temptation bundling...

Let's say you want to cook more meals at home. You're getting sick of fast food and want to develop the cooking habit.

Let's also suppose you love listening to a few select podcasts.

Can we bundle these things? Absolutely!

Give yourself permission to listen to your favorite podcasts while you cook meals. You get to indulge yourself while building a healthy habit.

That's temptation bundling in a nutshell. It's incredibly easy. And most importantly, it's effective.

Look, we both know it's hard to get excited about the things we need to do. But we can make them more appealing by packaging them with things we want to do.

It's a terrific way to build and reinforce new habits and routines.

So how do you get started?

Make two lists. One list should include every habit you'd like to adopt. The other list should include every indulgence that tempts you.

Don't hold back. Go crazy and list everything that comes to mind.

Then, start looking for ways to pair one item from the first list with one item from the second list.

Bundle those temptations!

You may be surprised by how quickly you build habits you've been procrastinating on.

That's it for today.

Let's talk soon,

Damon

P.S. Building the right habits can literally transform your life. If you'd like a step-by-step plan for adopting any habit you desire, check out my book Small Habits Revolution.

emails.subject: Here's a quick remedy for procrastination you can use right now
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I've written a lot about procrastination in the past. Namely, how to conquer it and take purposeful action toward your goals.

It may not be a sexy topic. But it's one that has a huge impact on our lives.

Today, I'm going to share a quick tip that I regularly use to get off my duff when I'm feeling lazy. This is what I do when my willpower is low and all I want to do is binge-watch Game of Thrones.

It's surprisingly simple.

I commit to a task for three minutes. I tell myself, "Self, just do this task for three minutes and then you can go back to being a couch potato."

Can you guess what happens?

Without fail, once I take action, I KEEP taking action.

Here's a real-life example...

I love to write. But sometimes I'm not in the mood. I'm lazy or just want to do something else.

So I commit to writing for three minutes.

Once those three minutes are up, do I quit?

Nope. Never. I keep going. I find my rhythm and continue writing, sometimes for hours.

Try it for yourself. The next time you're faced with a task you'd rather postpone, commit to doing it for three minutes.

It doesn't matter if it's yardwork, exercise, or something related to your job. Just do it for three minutes.

I'll bet you'll find your groove and do it longer.

Is this a permanent solution? Of course not. Ideally, you'll rely on habits to beat procrastination.

But when you're in a slump, this strategy works wonders. I promise.

That's it for today.

Let's talk soon,

Damon

P.S. Procrastination is a big problem that affects our happiness, self-esteem, and quality of life. If you regularly struggle to take action, check out my book The Procrastination Cure.

emails.subject: Are you keeping these 3 indispensable types of to-do lists?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

If you're like me, you keep a daily to-do list and a master to-do list.

The former keeps you on track and ensures you get the important stuff done.

The latter is a brain dump. It includes every item you can think of that warrants your attention.

Frankly, this master to-do list isn't very useful on a day-to-day basis. But it can be useful to look at each week, if only to stay on top of the tasks you consider crucial.

But there are lots of other to-do lists you may want to keep depending on your circumstances.

Here are three of them.

#1 - Project task list

This list is built around a particular project. Write down every task that needs to be fulfilled to bring the project to completion.

One advantage is that it gives you a terrific bird's-eye view of the project in question. Another advantage is that it unfailingly answers the question, "What's next?"

#2 - Activity-focused checklist

This list includes every item related to a recurring activity. The activity repeats, but not so often that it's easy to remember everything that needs to be done related to it.

An example is a travel packing checklist. If you plan to travel, you don't want to forget your phone, Kindle, adapters, chargers, sunglasses, toothbrush, and Chapstick. Put these items on your checklist and you'll never have to rely on your memory.

Personally, I'd be lost without my checklists. (My wife will attest to this.)

#3 - Entertainment lists

Leisure time is important. It's more than just pleasurable. It keeps us productive. The thing is, it's hard to keep track of everything we want to enjoy related to our leisure time.

To-do lists to the rescue!

Maintain one list for the books you'd like to read, one for the movies and TV shows you'd like to watch, one for the restaurants you'd like to visit, and even one for the recipes you'd like to try.

I use spreadsheets to keep track of this stuff. Todoist.com is also a great option. Use whatever tool works best for you. If you want to keep things "old school," pen and paper work just fine.

As you can imagine, there are many other types of helpful to-do lists. We'll get to them later. For now, think about whether the three types of lists above will make you more productive and organized.

If so, today's the perfect time to incorporate them into your task management system!

One last bit of advice: start small. Keep things simple. Then, build as your needs dictate.

That's it for now.

Let's talk soon!

Damon

P.S. I wrote a complete guide to creating to-do lists that work. It's called To-Do List Formula. It'll prove helpful if you're having trouble in this area.

emails.subject: The best way to deal with distractions for sharper focus
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

You've no doubt read advice suggesting that you eliminate distractions if you want to focus and get stuff done. I've given that advice myself.

It's solid counsel. It works.

But there's something else that's just as important. In fact, it's more important. It reveals how we react to distractions and the extent to which we let them affect us.

Once we're aware of these things, we can take purposeful action toward making positive, productive changes.

You see, distractions in and of themselves aren't terrible things. Studies show that, in the right circumstances, they can foster creativity, help us solve problems, and even improve our mood.

The problem is in how we react to distractions.

Too often, we let them completely dominate our headspace. They ruin our flow, wreak havoc with our concentration, and cause us to set aside our work.

How many times have you visited Facebook "for just a minute" only to find yourself clicking, scrolling, and reading a half hour later?

How many times have you tried to focus on something with your phone nearby only to find yourself checking every text that arrives?

Normally, I'd advise installing a site blocker in your browser to prevent you from visiting Facebook while you work.

And I'd advise turning off your phone when you need to focus to eliminate the temptation to check new texts and emails.

These are sensible steps to take.

But it's also important, more important in fact, to be aware of how and why you respond to certain distractions.

That's the key to controlling them instead of letting them control you.

Ultimately, you'll be able to choose when, where, and how you'll allow yourself to be distracted. Moreover, the distractions will be to your benefit rather than posing as annoying roadblocks to your focus and productivity.

Remember, distractions can be useful in the right circumstances.

How To Apply This To Your Life

Step 1: Over the next few weeks, identify the distractions that have the greatest impact on you. These are the ones for which you have true compulsions.

Maybe it's Facebook. Maybe it's your phone. Maybe it's Netflix. Whatever they are, write them down on a piece of paper (we're going old school here).

Step 2: Rate your level of compulsion as it relates to each distraction.

Write down a number between 1 and 5 next to each item. "1" means you can easily ignore the distraction. "5" means you'll drop everything to chase it.

Step 3: Exert control over your response to each distraction you've written down.

The goal is twofold. First, be mindful of why you respond to each distraction in the manner you typically do so. For example, do you reach for your phone whenever you're bored or stressed? It's useful to be aware of the triggers.

Second, get into the habit of resisting whatever compels you to pursue these distractions.

I'm not going to sugarcoat this. This is hard work. It takes time and can be frustrating.

But there's a wonderful upside. When you're aware of how and why you respond to certain distractions, you'll develop greater control over them. You'll be able to choose when, where, and how you'll allow them to affect you.

When that happens, you'll find that it becomes much easier to focus when you need to.

Talk to you soon,

Damon

P.S. If you'd like a complete soup-to-nuts guide for developing razor-sharp focus, check out my book Fast Focus.

我也會建議在需要專注時關掉手機,消除查看新簡訊和郵件的誘惑。

這些都是明智的做法。

但同樣重要——事實上更重要的是,要意識到自己為何以及如何回應特定的干擾。

這才是掌控干擾、而非被干擾掌控的關鍵。

最終,你將能夠選擇何時、何地、以何種方式讓自己被干擾。而且,這些干擾將對你有益,而不是成為阻礙你專注與生產力的惱人路障。

記住,在適當的情況下,干擾是可以派上用場的。

如何將這應用到你的生活中

第一步:在接下來的幾週內,找出對你影響最大的干擾。這些是你真正有強迫性衝動想去做的事。

也許是臉書,也許是手機,也許是 Netflix。無論是什麼,把它們寫在紙上(這裡我們要用老派的方法)。

第二步:針對每種干擾,為你的衝動程度評分。

在每個項目旁寫下 1 到 5 之間的數字。「1」代表你可以輕易忽略這個干擾,「5」代表你會放下一切去追逐它。

第三步:對你寫下的每個干擾,努力掌控自己的回應方式。

目標有兩個。首先,留意你為何會以慣常的方式回應每種干擾。舉例來說,你是不是無聊或有壓力時就會伸手拿手機?意識到這些觸發因素很有幫助。

第二,養成抵抗那些驅使你追逐這些干擾的衝動的習慣。

我不會粉飾太平——這是件辛苦的事,需要時間,而且可能令人沮喪。

但這麼做有個美好的回報。當你意識到自己為何以及如何回應特定干擾時,你就能對它們有更強的掌控力。你將能選擇何時、何地、以何種方式讓它們影響你。

到那時候,你會發現需要專注時會變得容易得多。

我們很快再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你想要一本從頭到尾培養敏銳專注力的完整指南,歡迎參考我的書《Fast Focus》。

emails.subject: How admitting you're wrong can (eventually) feel so right
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I have a confession to make...

I used to hate being wrong. Absolutely hate it.

Now, I realize that's not much of a confession. After all, who enjoys being wrong?

But I used to take it to whole 'nuther level. It wasn't enough for me to be right. I needed everyone to KNOW I was right.

... even if I was wrong.

Why?

Because if I was proven wrong, my entire sense of self would crumble.

That's the life of a perfectionist.

I know it because I lived it. My sense of self was so fragile that any suggestion that I was wrong felt like a threat.

And I was really good at attacking those threats.

If you're thinking, "Sheesh, you must have been a real pain to be around," you're right. I was.

It's embarrassing to think about today. Thankfully, my friends and loved ones are gracious enough to not rub my face in it.

The thing is, I know a lot of people struggle with the same issue. They feel like they need to be right. And even that's not enough for them.

They need others to know it.

Their sense of self depends on it.

If you can relate, there's a good chance you struggle with perfectionism. The two go hand in hand.

Well, I'd like to share a secret with you, from one (recovering) perfectionist to another: admitting you're wrong can be utterly liberating.

And not just admitting it, but EMBRACING it.

Obviously, this won't happen overnight. Personal growth never does. But it will happen over time with consistent effort.

If you wrestle with this problem, here's what I'd like you to do...

Think of a recent time when you and a friend or loved one disagreed about something. It should be a time when you really dug in your heels without good reason.

Maybe it was about a movie. Or a book. Perhaps it concerned politics. The topic doesn't matter.

Take this person aside and admit he or she made a good point.

Don't worry. I'm not asking you to make a huge mea culpa. You're simply acknowledging the fact that maybe, just maybe, your perspective wasn't as unassailable as you made it seem.

Remember, baby steps.

If you take the opportunity to do this on a regular basis, you'll find it gets easier.

And here's the crazy thing: the more you sincerely admit to being wrong, the stronger your sense of self will become.

With time, your confidence and self-worth won't depend on a shaky facade of infallibility. Instead, they'll stem from your ability to express yourself with poise and courage, and without feeling the need to defend your position whenever someone disagrees.

Again, it's completely liberating.

That's it for today. Now go tell someone you were wrong. :)

Damon

P.S. Perfectionism can be downright debilitating. I know from experience. If you too struggle with it, you might enjoy my book The Joy Of Imperfection.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

我要向你坦白一件事……

我曾經很討厭犯錯,徹頭徹尾地討厭。

現在我明白,這算不上什麼了不起的坦白,畢竟誰喜歡犯錯呢?

但我以前把這件事看得比一般人嚴重許多。光是我自己是對的還不夠,我需要每個人都「知道」我是對的。

……即使我其實是錯的。

為什麼?

因為如果被證明是錯的,我的整個自我認同就會崩潰。

這就是完美主義者的生活。

我知道,因為我親身經歷過。我的自我認同是如此脆弱,以至於任何暗示我犯錯的說法都像是一種威脅。

而我非常擅長攻擊這些「威脅」。

如果你心想:「天哪,你當時一定很難相處」,你說對了,我確實如此。

現在回想起來實在有點難為情。還好,我的朋友和摯愛夠寬容,沒有拿這件事來嘲諷我。

問題是,我知道很多人也有同樣的困擾。他們覺得自己必須是對的,而光是這樣還不夠。

他們需要別人知道這一點。

他們的自我認同仰賴於此。

如果你有同感,那麼你很可能也有完美主義的傾向。這兩者是相輔相成的。

好吧,身為一個(正在康復中的)完美主義者,我想跟你分享一個秘密:承認自己錯了,其實可以帶來徹底的解放感。

而且不只是承認,而是要真心「擁抱」它。

顯然,這不會一夜之間發生。個人成長從來都不是。但只要持續努力,隨著時間過去就會實現。

如果你也在和這個問題搏鬥,以下是我希望你去做的事……

想想最近一次你和朋友或摯愛因為某件事意見不合的情況。應該是那種你毫無充分理由卻堅持己見的時刻。

也許是關於一部電影,或一本書,也許是政治議題。話題本身不重要。

把這個人拉到一旁,承認他或她說得有道理。

別擔心,我不是要你做出什麼驚天動地的懺悔,你只是在承認一個事實:也許,只是也許,你的觀點並不像你表現出來的那樣無懈可擊。

記住,要一小步一小步來。

如果你經常抓住機會這樣做,你會發現它會越來越容易。

而且有件很神奇的事:你越真誠地承認自己犯錯,你的自我認同就會變得越堅強。

隨著時間過去,你的自信和自我價值將不再依賴那個搖搖欲墜的「永遠正確」的假象,而是源自於你能夠從容且勇敢地表達自己,不必在別人不同意時感到需要捍衛自己的立場。

再說一次,這種感覺完全是解放的。

今天就先到這裡。現在就去告訴某個人,你錯了。:)

Damon

P.S. 完美主義可能真的會讓人身心俱疲,我是過來人。如果你也在為此所苦,或許會喜歡我的書《The Joy Of Imperfection》。

emails.subject: Here's why (and when) you should abandon your productivity system
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

If you're like me, you start each morning with a daily to-do list. It shows you the tasks that require your attention along with their respective priorities.

When you have a lot to do during the day, this list is pure gold.

It keeps you focused. It helps you to stay on track.

If you stick to your list, crossing items out as you complete them, you can become a productivity beast, finishing every important task that's on your plate.

But what if a massive project is looming over you? It's not something you can simply slot onto your calendar and into your to-do list.

For example, suppose you're thinking about starting a business. It involves making a ton of crucial decisions.

You have to choose a corporate structure, consider financing options, think about whether and when to hire employees, create an online presence, and develop a marketing strategy.

And that's just the tip of the iceberg.

It's not something you can put on your calendar from 1:30 to 2:30. Nor should you put "think about starting a business" on your daily to-do list. It's too large an endeavor.

Ultimately, sticking to a traditional productivity system won't get it done.

Here's my solution...

Pick one day of the week and abandon your productivity system. Forget about your calendar and daily to-do list. Forget about using the Eisenhower Matrix to prioritize tasks. Forget about Kanban.

Set these things aside. Instead, use this one day of the week to focus exclusively on the big stuff.

Don't respond to emails. Don't return phone calls. Don't schedule appointments. Don't complete tasks to move small projects forward.

In short, don't work on anything that's unrelated to the "Big Project."

During this "free" day, you'll undoubtedly think of lots of items that need your attention. Just write them down. Then forget about them. You can address them tomorrow, prioritizing each one and placing them onto context-appropriate to-do lists.

This is the best way I've found to move BIG projects forward. I'm able to focus on them, giving them the time and attention they deserve. The result is that I can make a ton of progress in a relatively short time.

Remember, your productivity system is supposed to make your life better. It's supposed to help you get the important stuff done.

Sometimes, that means abandoning it for a day.

Try it. See for yourself whether doing so helps you to complete the Big Projects that are lingering on your plate.

I'm willing to bet you'll see terrific results.

Talk to you next time,

Damon

P.S. If you don't yet have a productivity system in place, you may find my book The 30-Day Productivity Plan useful. If you do, you might also enjoy Volume II.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

如果你和我一樣,每天早上都會從一份每日待辦清單開始。它會告訴你需要關注的任務以及它們各自的優先順序。

當一天要做的事很多時,這份清單簡直是無價之寶。

它讓你保持專注,幫助你不偏離軌道。

如果你堅持照著清單做,完成一項就劃掉一項,你就能變成生產力猛獸,完成手上每一項重要任務。

但如果有一個龐大的專案正籠罩著你呢?那不是你能簡單地排進行事曆和待辦清單裡的東西。

舉例來說,假設你正考慮創業。這牽涉到大量關鍵決策。

你必須選擇公司結構、考慮融資方式、思考是否以及何時聘用員工、建立線上形象,並擬定行銷策略。

而這還只是冰山一角。

這不是你能安排在行事曆上 1:30 到 2:30 之間完成的事,你也不該把「思考創業」寫在每日待辦清單上,這個任務太龐大了。

最終,死守傳統的生產力系統是完成不了這件事的。

以下是我的解決方案……

選一週中的一天,拋開你的生產力系統。忘掉你的行事曆和每日待辦清單,忘掉用艾森豪矩陣來排序任務,忘掉看板方法。

把這些都先擱在一邊。相反地,利用這一天,專心只處理大事。

不要回覆郵件,不要回電話,不要安排約會,不要去完成推進小型專案的任務。

簡而言之,不要處理任何與「大專案」無關的事。

在這個「自由」的一天裡,你一定會想到很多需要關注的事項。把它們寫下來就好,然後先拋在腦後。你可以明天再處理,依序排定優先順序,放進對應情境的待辦清單中。

這是我發現推進大型專案最好的方法。我能夠專注在它們上面,給予它們應得的時間與關注。結果是,我能在相對短的時間內取得大量進展。

記住,你的生產力系統本該讓你的生活變得更好,它應該幫助你完成重要的事。

有時候,這意味著要把它拋開一天。

試試看吧,親自體驗這麼做是否能幫助你完成那些遲遲未完成的大專案。

我敢打賭你會看到很棒的成果。

下次再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你還沒有建立生產力系統,你可能會覺得我的書《The 30-Day Productivity Plan》很實用。如果你已經讀過了,或許也會喜歡《Volume II》。

emails.subject: Is doing less the secret to accomplishing more?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Think of the "big wins" you've experienced in your life.

These are the moments you look back on and think to yourself, "Wow. I actually did that!" You feel proud and maybe even a little astonished.

One of my "big wins" came in the form of writing my first book. Another was losing 50 lb. when I was in high school.

I can't help but feel a deep sense of personal satisfaction whenever I think of those deeds.

But here's the thing...

Those accomplishment were only possible because I abandoned a bunch of things that were unimportant to me at the time.

I set them aside. Some temporarily. Some permanently.

And I focused on the stuff that truly mattered to me.

I'll bet you've had the same experience. Your biggest wins were likely made possible because you focused on them, so much so that you ignored things that were trivial to you.

What's more, I'll bet you found that ignoring the trivial stuff didn't pose a catastrophe. In fact, it probably had zero ill effect on your life at all.

That's why I think one of the secrets to accomplishing more is doing less. By abandoning unimportant matters, we conserve our attentional resources for the significant stuff.

That's how our big wins happen.

With that in mind, here's a quick exercise I encourage you to do today.

Step 1: List every project and commitment you have on your plate.

Include those that are current as well as those planned for the near future. Here are a few examples to get the juices flowing...

- declutter your closet
- clean out your garage
- read personal development books
- learn to speak a new language
- create a presentation for your job
- attend a business conference
- take a cooking class
- learn to play the guitar
- write a book
- design an app
- start a side business
- build a website
- plan a family vacation
- join a softball league

Step 2: Select three projects from the list.

Put a star by them so they stand out. These three projects are the ones that mean the most to you right now.

Step 3: Identify the projects that can be placed on the back burner.

Put an "X" by them. These are the items you can abandon, at least temporarily, without suffering a crisis.

Step 4: Identify the projects that have neither a star nor an "X" by them.

These items need your attention, but aren't the ones that excite you.

An example might be to create a presentation for your job. Or replace a toilet in your upstairs bathroom. These things need to get done, even if they won't deliver the sense of personal satisfaction offered by the three projects you select in Step 3.

Step 5: Come up with an action plan for addressing each project you identified in Step 4.

The idea is to get them off your plate. That way, you can focus on the good stuff, the things that excite you.

Ultimately, being productive - or heck, being HAPPY - isn't about getting tons of things done. It's about accomplishing things that are important to you.

The fastest way to do that is to get the trivial stuff off your plate.

That's it for now.

Talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you'd like to do a deeper dive into this concept, you may enjoy reading my book 80/20 Your Life!

第五步:為第四步中找出的每個專案擬定行動計畫。

目標是把它們從你的待辦清單上清掉,這樣你就能專注在真正美好、令你興奮的事情上。

說到底,所謂的高效率——或者說,所謂的「快樂」——並不是要完成一大堆事情,而是要完成對你來說重要的事情。

實現這個目標最快的方法,就是把瑣事從你的待辦清單上清除。

這次就先到這裡。

談後再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你想更深入了解這個概念,或許會喜歡閱讀我的書《80/20 Your Life!》。

emails.subject: Pop quiz: are you too nice?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Let's get something out of the way upfront: there's absolutely nothing wrong with being nice. Far from it.

Being generous with our time, considerate with our actions, and willing to help out when we're asked are practically virtues.

Besides, doing so feels good.

We feel connected to the people we're helping. We identify and empathize with them.

When a friend asks us to take him to the airport, we want to be there for him because we know what it's like to need a ride somewhere.

When a neighbor asks us to help her move, we want to help because we can sympathize with the stress and uncertainty that accompanies moving.

When a family member asks us to help him resolve a problem, we're willing to set everything aside because we understand what it's like to need someone to turn to.

But is it possible that you're TOO nice? And if so, are people taking advantage of your kindness?

Today, let's cover a few telltale signs that suggest you're going far beyond the call of duty to please others. Why? Because you may be setting yourself up to be taken for granted.

Sign #1: You feel terrible whenever you say no to someone.

Sign #2: You often regret saying yes, and feel resentful afterward.

Sign #3: You're always available for people, regardless of what's on your plate.

Sign #4: You're afraid of confrontation.

Sign #5: You never have time for yourself.

Sign #6: You feel you don't deserve to take time for yourself.

Sign #7: You fear being rejected by others.

I'll bet you can relate to at least one of the above "symptoms" of being too nice. I have personal experience with all of them.

The good news is, once you recognize the problem, you can take steps to correct it. The first step is learning how to say no.

That's it for today. Short and sweet.

Let's talk soon,

Damon

P.S. If you're not sure how to say no to people, you might enjoy my book The Art Of Saying NO. It leaves nothing to the imagination.
emails.contentZh:

慷慨付出時間、行事體貼、在被請求時願意伸出援手,幾乎可以說是一種美德。

而且,這麼做感覺很好。

徵兆 #1:每當你對某人說不時,你都感到很糟糕。

徵兆 #2:你經常後悔自己答應了別人,事後感到怨懟。

徵兆 #3:無論你手上有多少事,你總是有空幫別人的忙。

徵兆 #4:你害怕正面衝突。

徵兆 #5:你從來沒有時間留給自己。

徵兆 #6:你覺得自己不配擁有屬於自己的時間。

徵兆 #7:你害怕被別人拒絕。

我敢打賭,以上「太友善」的症狀裡,你至少能認同一項。而我自己則是每一項都親身經歷過。

好消息是,一旦你意識到問題所在,就能採取行動來改正它。第一步,就是學會如何說「不」。

今天就到這裡,簡短扼要。

我們很快再聊,

Damon

P.S. 如果你不確定該怎麼對別人說不,你可能會喜歡我的書《The Art Of Saying NO》,書裡把一切都講得清清楚楚,不留任何想像空間。

emails.subject: Here are 5 things I do each morning to start my day on the right foot
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

My mornings dictate my productivity.

If I have a good morning, if I'm relaxed and purposeful, I end up getting a lot of stuff done as the day progresses. If my morning is chaotic, the rest of the day follows suit.

I'll bet you can relate.

The good news is, we have a lot of control over our mornings. That means we can set ourselves up for success.

It's just a matter of embracing simple habits that work for us.

Below are five things I do each morning to get the day started in the right direction. They're a part of my morning routine.

1. I stay unplugged for 20 minutes.

The moment I get online or check my phone, I find myself in a reactive state. Emails, texts, and social media demand attention. So I take 20 minutes to be present and mindful.

2. I write morning pages.

Morning pages are like a journal. The difference is, you have a lot more latitude. You basically write down whatever is in your head. It's like opening a pressure value in your mind where your fears, concerns, and ideas spill out.

It's cathartic and calming.

3. I make the bed.

I know, it sounds a little silly. After all, making the bed is such a small thing. But it gives me a quick sense of accomplishment. It's an action I can take immediately that delivers a desired result.

That puts me in a good frame of mind.

4. I perform stretches.

Two minutes. That's all it takes. The upside is that it loosens my joints, gets my blood flowing, and helps me to feel energized.

5. I express gratitude.

I'm embarrassed to say I take a lot for granted. It's an easy habit to get into. So I spend a few moments each morning thinking about the things I'm grateful for.

That includes my wife and family, our home, and the fact that people enjoy the books I write. The list is long.

Contemplating this stuff puts me in a terrific mood!

I'm not suggesting you do everything I do in the morning. But if you're like me, you enjoy trying things and seeing whether they work for you.

In that spirit, I encourage you to experiment with the five things I listed above. Note how each one makes you feel.

Keep what works and chuck the rest!

That's it for now. I'll talk to you soon,

Damon

P.S. If your current morning routine consists of dragging yourself out of bed and stumbling to your coffeemaker, it may be time for a Morning Makeover. :)
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

我的早晨決定了我的生產力。

如果我有一個美好的早晨——放鬆而有目標——隨著這一天的展開,我最終會完成很多事情。如果我的早晨一團混亂,接下來的一整天也會跟著混亂。

我敢打賭你也有同感。

好消息是,我們對自己的早晨其實有很大的掌控力,這代表我們可以為成功做好準備。

這只是個養成適合自己的簡單習慣的問題。

以下是我每天早上做的五件事,幫助我把這一天導向正確的方向。它們是我晨間例行公事的一部分。

1. 我保持離線 20 分鐘。

一旦我上網或查看手機,我就會陷入一種被動反應的狀態。郵件、簡訊和社群媒體都在要求我的注意力。所以我會花 20 分鐘保持當下、保持專注。

這既能宣洩情緒,也能讓人平靜下來。

我知道,這聽起來有點傻。畢竟,整理床鋪是件小事。但它能給我一種快速的成就感。這是一件我可以立即採取行動、並得到預期結果的事。

本著這樣的精神,我鼓勵你試試上面列出的這五件事。留意每一件事帶給你的感受。

有效的就保留,沒效的就丟掉!

這次就先到這裡,我們很快再聊,

Damon

emails.subject: Why you should use time chunks to optimize your leisure time
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

The last couple of emails were pretty long. So let's take it easy this time around. :)

Let's briefly talk about time chunks.

We usually talk about them in the context of getting things done. When we block off chunks of time, we're able to focus better, ignore distractions, and get into the zone.

... all of which result in greater productivity.

But we should also use time chunks to schedule our leisure time.

Why?

Because if we just "let things happen," we end up spending our free time on meaningless activities.

Things like watching television or aimlessly surfing the internet. Or worse, worrying about stuff we can't control.

That leads to boredom and stress, both of which make us unhappy.

Personally, I'm happiest when I'm engaged and challenged by whatever I'm doing, and making use of my skills. When I spend time watching television and surfing the internet, I feel unstimulated and dissatisfied.

Perhaps you're the same way.

If so, you might enjoy using a tactic I've been using to optimize my free time: I use time chunks to schedule leisure activities.

For example, I visit a local park at the same time nearly every day to read. I play online chess at the same time each afternoon.

By scheduling my free time, I'm less likely to end up doing activities that fail to stimulate me.

Try it for yourself.

Instead of just "letting things happen" when you have free time, use time chunks to plan things.

I realize this may seem counterintuitive. After all, planning is for work, not play.

But I'd be willing to bet you'll find this approach makes you feel happier and more satisfied over the long run!

Leisurely yours,

Damon

P.S. If you're not sure how to use time chunks, don't panic. I've written a short, useful guide that provides the nuts and bolts. Check out my book The Time Chunking Method.
