emails.subject: Here's a 3-step strategy for decluttering your home
emails.contentEn:
Hi 張振輝,

Have you ever tried to declutter your home, but found yourself unwilling to get rid of things?

If so, you're not alone. I've received three emails over the last few weeks from subscribers who are struggling with this very challenge.

Most recently, subscriber Kay (I've changed her name because... privacy) wrote:

"My biggest challenge is that I know I need to downsize my possessions to achieve the greater simplicity and order in my life that I want. But deciding which items to release is slowing my progress down. I invariably pick up an item and decide 'but I will probably need this', and end up making no progress. I need to break my indecision cycle so I can make progress toward my goal."

I thought my advice to Kay might prove helpful to you, too. Here's what I told her:

Hey Kay. Awhile back I went through a major declutter at home. I had a truckload of things to get rid of. Like you, I was afraid to discard of a lot of things. A little voice in my head kept telling me "You're going to need that someday. Don't you dare toss it."

I needed to silence that voice. Here's what worked for me...

First, I made a simple rule: if I hadn't read or used an item in the last six months, that item automatically became a candidate for disposal.

Second, I reminded myself that if I truly needed something after I had gotten rid of it, I could reacquire it. I might have to buy it again, but I resigned myself to that possibility. This step was incredibly freeing for me. It allowed me to abandon my fears about discarding things I might (but probably wouldn't) need in the future.

Third, I committed to getting rid of three things each day. Three felt doable since I could get it done within a couple minutes. As the weeks passed, I became more comfortable with tossing things out. Action begets action. And so three items per day became four, and then five, and so on.

Little by little, my home became less and less cluttered. :)

You may have noticed that I'm a big advocate of making slow, incremental progress. I'd rather be the tortoise than the hare in Aesop's fable. It makes big projects like decluttering your home a lot less daunting.

If you want to get rid of possessions that are just taking up space, but are struggling with letting them go, try the method I used. It takes time, but it works!

Add this task to your morning routine. It only takes a couple minutes so it won't seem like you're putting in much effort. But over the next few weeks, you'll be blown away by how much stuff you'll have tossed out.

Let me know how it goes!
Damon

P.S. If you'd like to learn how to create morning routines, check out my book Morning Makeover.

emails.subject: 5 ways to crush your deadlines
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I learned something interesting the other day.

During the Civil War, prison camp guards would draw a line on the ground. They'd call it a deadline. Any prisoner who crossed it would be shot. Shot dead, to be specific. Hence, the term.

Thankfully, we're less serious about deadlines these days. But it got me thinking.

Maybe we need to be more serious about them. After all, many of us treat deadlines like suggestions rather than actual time limits.

For example:
- Students regularly ask for extensions on class assignments.
- Executives often finish projects long after they're due.
- Freelancers routinely deliver work late to clients.

Some of us are always late buying birthday gifts. Others are late paying their taxes. Still others are late in getting their vehicles serviced.

Missing deadlines is practically a way of life.

Humorist Douglas Adams once said, "I love deadlines. I love the whooshing noise they make as they go by." That's funny because it carries a note of truth. Most of us can relate to the sentiment.

But suppose you're tired of missing deadlines and would like to start taking them seriously. Here are 5 ways to make it happen.

1. Announce the deadline to others.
Make yourself accountable. No one likes to fail in front of other people.

2. Plan your work.
Break projects down to their individual tasks. Estimate how long each task will take you to complete. Be conservative with your estimates.

3. Accelerate the deadline.
If a project is due on Friday, plan to finish it by Wednesday. Give yourself a buffer. It may come in handy.

4. Monitor all projects and deadlines in one place.
If you have an iPhone, try the calendar app Fantastical 2. If you have an Android phone, aCalendar may fit the bill. Personally, I like Google Calendar. It's simple and free (and I love free).

5. Start.
This might sound silly. But ask yourself: how many times have you postponed a project only to scramble at the last minute to get it done on time? I'm not pointing fingers. I've done it more times than I can count. But I've found that if I start working on a project right away, I'm likely to finish it early.

Try these five tips if you're sick of missing your deadlines. I guarantee they'll help!

Talk to you soon,
Damon

P.S. If you're looking for a way to organize your workflow so you're better able to hit your deadlines, check out my book The Time Chunking Method.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

南北戰爭期間,戰俘營的守衛會在地上劃一條線,稱之為「deadline」(死線)。任何跨過這條線的囚犯都會被槍殺——確切地說,是被打死。這就是這個詞的由來。

所幸現在我們對待「死線」已經沒那麼認真了。但這讓我開始思考。

也許我們應該對它更認真一點。畢竟,我們很多人把截止日期當成建議,而不是真正的時間限制。

舉例來說:
—學生經常要求延後繳交作業。
—主管常常在專案到期很久之後才完成。
—自由工作者經常延遲交付作品給客戶。

我們有些人總是拖到最後才買生日禮物,有些人拖延繳稅,還有些人拖著不去保養車輛。

錯過截止日期幾乎已經成了一種生活方式。

幽默作家道格拉斯·亞當斯曾說:「我喜歡截止日期,我喜歡它們呼嘯而過的聲音。」這句話之所以好笑,是因為它帶有一絲真實。我們大多數人都能感同身受。

但假設你已經厭倦了錯過截止日期,想開始認真對待它們,以下是5個實現方法。

1. 向他人公開你的截止日期。

5. 開始行動。

emails.subject: A nifty Todoist tip you can use today
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

If you've read any of my books, you'll recall that I use Todoist. It's a fantastic app that makes it a snap to manage your to-do lists.

It works on every platform. That means you can use it on a Mac or Windows machine. It also works in every browser. Google Chrome, Firefox, Opera, Safari, Internet Explorer... take your pick. The app works every time. And did I mention it's completely free?

Anywho, I stumbled onto a neat little Todoist "trick" a couple weeks ago. It's something that I found to be really useful. I figured you might get some mileage out of it, too.

First, I'll explain the "trick." Then, I'll tell you how I used it. That may give you some ideas on how you can use it to improve your workflow.

If you use Todoist, you probably know that it understands natural language. For example, suppose you have a task that's due next Tuesday. You can plug in Tuesday's date if you prefer. But you can just easily type "next Tuesday." Todoist will automatically assign the appropriate due date.

You can also type things like this:
- in 4 days (four days from today)
- mid June (June 15th)
- next week (next Monday by default, but you can modify this in Todoist's settings)

This also works for recurring tasks on Todoist. For example, suppose you have a task that you perform every Wednesday. One option is to manually add the task to your to-do list each week. But that's a hassle.

Todoist allows you to plug in "every Wed," and it'll take care of the rest. You don't have to add the task manually each week. Todoist will do it for you.

You can also type things like this:
- every 3 days
- every month
- every Mon and Fri

Todoist will take care of the rest. Pretty nifty, right?

But I haven't even gotten to the "trick" I discovered. Here it is...

Some recurring tasks end after a set period of time. You do them for awhile, and then you stop. When that day comes, you no longer want these tasks to appear on your to-do lists.

Todoist gives you a way to automatically purge them on any date you choose. All you have to do is type something like "every Tues until July 27." On July 27, Todoist will get rid of the recurring task in question.

Here's how I recently used this feature. Every time I release a new book, I schedule ads to run in various email newsletters. I need to verify that the ads ran properly the day after they were supposed to. So one of my daily to-do items during this period is to "verify email ads."

After two weeks, the ads run their course, and there's nothing left for me to verify. So I no longer want to see this to-do item on my daily list.

Todoist solved this problem for me. Here's how... After releasing my most recent book, I created the "verify email ads" task in Todoist, as usual. I then typed in "every day for two weeks" for the due date.

The task showed up every day on my main to-do list, as expected. But after two weeks, it was gone. Poof! Like magic. Easy peasy.

If you've never used Todoist, I urge you to take it for a test drive. It won't cost you a penny. And I'm willing to bet it'll help you to better manage your to-do lists. It sure made a difference in my workflow!

When you do try Todoist, experiment with some of the "due date" language above. It's kinda fun and really useful!

That's it for now.

Talk to you soon,
Damon

P.S. If your to-do lists are out of control, grab a copy of my book To-Do List Formula. I guarantee it'll help.

emails.subject: Is this simple mistake destroying your focus?
emails.contentEn:
Tell me if this sounds familiar...

Your head is fuzzy. Your thoughts are scattered. You're distracted, and having a tough time concentrating on your work.

As a result, little is getting done.

Worse, the work you are managing to finish is pretty shoddy. You're going to have to do some serious revisions.

Then there's the inevitable guilt. Guilt for allowing yourself to be so easily distracted. Guilt for wasting time. Guilt for producing sloppy work.

Now, imagine this scenario...

You're hyper-focused. You're able to concentrate and completely ignore distractions. As a result, you're getting a ton of work done!

And the best part? You're putting out high-quality work. The type of work you'll be proud to show others.

As for guilt, there is none. Zilch. Zippo. You end the day feeling present, productive, and satisfied.

There are lots of factors that dictate which scenario you experience on a daily basis. One of the most common is sleep. Specifically, the amount and quality.

If you're not getting enough sleep, or you suffer from poor sleep, it's going to be almost impossible to stay focused during the day.

Here are 3 "quick win" ideas for making sure you get the amount of high-quality sleep you need each night...

1. Go to bed an hour early.
If you've been cutting corners on your sleep, your brain is probably more tired than you realize. Do yourself a favor and hit the sack early. Don't watch TV in bed. Don't eat last-minute snacks. If anything, read a book. You'll probably feel drowsy within minutes.

2. Stop "binge watching" Netflix.
I get it. It's tough to stop watching Daredevil, Orange Is The New Black, and Gilmore Girls. Your brain keeps telling you, "C'mon, just one more episode." But if binge watching TV shows is cutting into your sleep time, turn them off. They're not going anywhere. Your favorite shows will be there tomorrow.

3. Read in bed.
I love reading before bed. It makes me feel relaxed. Even if I'm reading a horror novel, my mind feels strangely at ease. When it's time to turn out the lights, I'm snoring within minutes (my wife can vouch for that last part!).

Try it. Instead of watching TV, responding to email, or playing with your phone while you're in bed, read a book. Let your brain unwind. I'd be willing to bet you'll fall asleep faster and sleep more soundly. And that will only improve your focus the following day.

"Restfully" yours,
Damon
emails.contentZh:

1. 提早一小時上床睡覺。

3. 在床上看書。
我喜歡睡前閱讀,這讓我感覺放鬆。即使是在讀恐怖小說,我的心也奇怪地感到平靜。到了該熄燈的時候,我幾分鐘內就會打呼(我太太可以為這最後一點作證!)。

emails.subject: Eat the frog to cure your to-do list blues
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Take a look at your to-do list. I'll bet there's at least one task that's causing you major grief.

Maybe it's that Powerpoint presentation you're supposed to prepare for your boss.

Maybe it's that early-morning jog you promised yourself you'd do.

Or maybe it's a client project that's boring you to tears, and every minute you spend on it is a battle.

Whatever it is, do that task first. Do it before you do any of the other items on your to-do list.

That's called "eating the frog." It comes from a quote by Mark Twain:

"If it's your job to eat a frog, it's best to do it first thing in the morning. And if it's your job to eat two frogs, it's best to eat the biggest one first."

Twain is saying that you should do the worst item on your to-do list before you tackle anything else. Get it out of the way. Otherwise, it'll hang over your head like a dark cloud.

Try it. Identify the task that's causing you the most aggravation. Get it done and scratch it off your list.

I guarantee it'll put you in a better mood. And that'll make the rest of your day flow more smoothly!

Talk to you soon,
Damon

emails.subject: 5 ways to prevent your phone from distracting you
emails.contentEn:
I was at Starbucks the other day and was taken aback by something I witnessed. As I ordered my Caffè Americano and settled into my work, I watched the folks around me.

Some were talking to friends.
Some were working on laptops.
Some were reading books, magazines, and newspapers.
Nearly all of them had one thing in common: they allowed their phones to interrupt whatever they were doing.
The talkers interrupted their conversations to read new texts.
The laptop warriors interrupted their work to take unimportant calls (I may have been eavesdropping).
The readers interrupted their reading to check Facebook and Instagram.
I even saw folks at the register stop ordering drinks to read and respond to texts, even though people waited in line behind them!
Maybe you can relate. You may even feel as if your phone has commandeered your life.
The good news is, there are simple things you can do to reclaim your freedom. If your phone's chirps, beeps, and ringing are wreaking havoc with your ability to focus, try these 5 tips...
1. Let voicemail do its job. Don't have time to take a call? Let it roll to voicemail. That's what it's there for.
2. Go into Total Silence mode. Android devices have a Total Silence feature. iPhones have a Do Not Disturb feature. They do the same thing: silence ringing and notifications.
3. Schedule your phone use. Don't be a reactive phone user, taking calls and responding to texts and emails as they arrive. Instead, designate two or three 20-minute periods during your day to address them. Put them on your calendar.
4. Ignore unknown callers. Unfamiliar numbers are usually salespeople or folks conducting consumer surveys.
5. Leave your phone off when you're with someone. If you're spending time with a friend or loved one, be present with that person. Don't allow your phone to interrupt your time together.
Do these five things and I guarantee you'll find it easier to focus and stay productive.

Talk to you soon,
Damon

emails.subject: Is social media hurting your focus?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I've long suspected that Facebook, Twitter, and other social media sites hurt our ability to concentrate. Not just while we're browsing them, but even after we leave them behind.

That's the case for me, at least.

After spending time on Facebook, I always find that it's difficult to concentrate. I literally have to close my eyes, take a few deep breaths, and clear my head before I can truly dial in and focus on my work.

I recently watched a TEDx talk given by Cal Newport that explains why this problem occurs. It's fascinating and makes a lot of sense. You can watch the talk on Youtube. It's short (just under 14 minutes) and filled with solid insight.

Newport is the bestselling author of the book Deep Work. It's an impressive book on the subject of focus. I think his ideas regarding how social media affects our brains are absolutely correct. Watch his TEDx talk and judge for yourself.

If you're addicted to social media, I recommend taking these five steps to break its hold on you:

Step #1: Delete social media apps from your phone.
Step #2: Take the weekends off. Only check in Monday through Friday.
Step #3: Don't browse aimlessly. Have a purpose for checking in.
Step #4: Set rules. For example, no social media before noon.
Step #5: Give yourself 15 minutes. Then, log off.

Do the above consistently, and you'll gradually wean yourself off of Facebook, Twitter, and the like. Don't be surprised if you feel more relaxed, less impulsive, and better able to focus as a result!

Talk to you soon,
Damon

emails.subject: "No."
emails.contentEn:
It's such a simple, unpretentious word. So why do many of us have trouble saying it to others, even at the cost of our productivity?

Here's my story:

I used to be a yes-man.

If you asked me to do something, I'd do it. If you needed me, I was there. I wanted to please people, even if that meant sacrificing or postponing activities that were important to me.

Maybe it had something to do with a fear of rejection. Or maybe I just didn't want to disappoint people. I'm sure a psychologist would have a field day examining the psyche of my youth.

Regardless of its origin, this desperate tendency to please eventually became a behavioral pattern. I was like one of Pavlov's dogs. If you asked for my help, I instinctively said "yes."

You can imagine how that affected my productivity. I spent so much time catering to others that I had little time left over to address my own work.

Can you relate to this problem?

Here's how to fix it:

Step #1: Recognize that saying "yes" imposes an opportunity cost.

Saying "yes" to one person means saying "no" to someone else, including yourself. For example, if you help a friend move, you won't be able to spend that time with your family.

Step #2: Stall for time.

When someone asks you to commit to something, don't respond with an immediate "yes" or "no." Instead, tell the person you'll review your calendar and get back to him or her. That'll give you time to evaluate your priorities and decide whether the commitment fits in your schedule.

Step #3: Be firm and unapologetic.

Don't waver when you say "no." Don't apologize. And don't make up excuses. Be respectful, but firm. If you're asked for a reason, simply say, "I'd rather not spend my available time doing that."

Remember, as long as you're sincere and respectful, you're not responsible for the other person's disappointment, hurt feelings, or resentment.

Step #4: Provide a time frame.

If you decide to help someone, give him or her a time frame that indicates your limited availability. For example, don't just say "Sure. I'll help you with that." Instead, say "I can help you with that from 1:00 p.m. to 1:20 p.m. Does that work?"

If you're a people pleaser, saying "no" can be uncomfortable. But trust me. It gets easier the more you do it. And here's the exciting part: the more you say "no" to others, the more you'll be able to say "yes" to yourself!

Let's talk soon,
Damon Zahariades

P.S. The negative effects of habitually saying "yes" are covered in my book The Art Of Saying NO. It also provides a strategic guide for setting strict boundaries and earning others' respect in the process!

不管起因為何,這種急切討好他人的傾向最終變成了一種行為模式。我就像巴夫洛夫的狗一樣——只要有人開口請我幫忙,我就本能地說「好」。

你可以想像這對我的生產力造成了什麼影響。我花太多時間去滿足別人,留給自己工作的時間所剩無幾。

你是不是也有同樣的困擾?

以下是解決方法:

第一步:認清說「好」是有機會成本的。

對一個人說「好」,就等於對另一個人(包括你自己)說「不」。舉例來說,如果你幫朋友搬家,你就沒辦法把那段時間留給家人。

第二步:先拖延一下。

當有人要求你答應某件事時,不要立刻回答「好」或「不好」。告訴對方你要先看看行事曆再回覆。這樣你就有時間評估自己的優先順序,判斷這件事是否適合排進你的行程。

第三步:態度堅定,不必道歉。

說「不」的時候不要動搖,不要道歉,也不要編藉口。保持尊重,但態度堅定。如果對方問你原因,只需說:「我比較想把時間留給別的事。」

記住,只要你真誠且有禮貌地拒絕,對方的失望、受傷或不滿都不是你的責任。

第四步:給出明確的時間範圍。

如果你決定幫忙某人,就給對方一個能反映你有限時間的範圍。舉例來說,不要只說「當然,我會幫你」,而是說:「我可以在下午 1:00 到 1:20 幫你,這樣可以嗎?」

如果你是個習慣討好別人的人,說「不」可能會讓你感到不自在。但相信我,做得越多就越容易。而且令人興奮的是:你越常對別人說「不」,就越能對自己說「好」!

改天聊,
戴蒙・查哈里亞德斯

附註:習慣性說「好」帶來的負面影響,我在我的書《The Art Of Saying NO》中有詳細探討。這本書也提供了設定嚴格界線、同時贏得他人尊重的策略指南!

emails.subject: How attention residue harms your focus...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Have you ever stopped working on a task to address another one only to find that when you return to the first task that it's tough to focus and regain your momentum?

You're not alone. It happens to everyone.

It's due to something called attention residue. Here's how it works:

Let's say you're working on a report for your job. You're in the zone and making great headway on it. In fact, you're confident you can finish it by lunchtime.

Suddenly, your phone rings. The call might be important, so you pick it up. It lasts a few minutes, and you hang up the receiver and get back to work.

Unfortunately, you find it's not a smooth transition. Your momentum has been broken. You're no longer in the zone. You stare at the report and struggle to get back on track.

Sound familiar? Here's what happened:

The phone call left behind some "residue" on your consciousness. This residue subtly demanded your attention, preventing you from refocusing on the report. It caused your brain to experience the cognitive equivalent of getting your tires stuck in the mud.

According to smarter folks than I, this effect is the reason distractions and interruptions are so costly in terms of our productivity. They destroy our ability to concentrate.

What's the solution?

First, create an environment that allows you to work free from distractions. Turn off your phone. If you have an office, close the door. If you work in a cubicle, let your co-workers know you'd prefer to work undisturbed for a set period of time. If you work from home and someone knocks on your front door, ignore it.

Second, work in time chunks. Work for 30 minutes and take a 5-minute break. Or work for 50 minutes and take a 10-minute. It's up to you. You decide the length of your work sessions and breaks.

Third, commit to single-tasking. Work on one task per time chunk. No more.

That's it. Do those three things and you'll be less encumbered by attention residue. Think of how much more productive you'll be when you're finally able to focus!

Next time, I'll share a simple tip that'll give you more control of your day. It may not be easy, but it's definitely effective.

Stay tuned and have a great week!

Damon Zahariades
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

你是否曾經停下手邊的工作去處理另一件事,結果回來繼續做原本那件事時,卻發現很難重新集中精神、找回節奏?

你不是唯一有這種經驗的人,每個人都會遇到這種狀況。

這是因為一種叫做「注意力殘留」(attention residue)的現象。運作方式是這樣的:

假設你正在為工作寫一份報告。你進入了心流狀態,進展順利,甚至有信心能在午餐前完成。

突然,你的手機響了。這通電話可能很重要,於是你接了起來。講了幾分鐘後,你掛上電話,回頭繼續工作。

但你會發現,這個轉換並不順暢。你的節奏被打斷了,你不再處於心流狀態。你盯著報告,卻很難重新進入狀況。

聽起來很熟悉嗎?這是發生了什麼事:

那通電話在你的意識裡留下了一些「殘留物」。這些殘留物悄悄地佔據你的注意力,讓你無法重新專注在報告上。它讓你的大腦體驗到近似「輪胎陷進泥巴裡」的認知狀態。

根據比我更懂這方面的專家所言,這正是為什麼干擾和打斷對我們的生產力代價如此高昂——它們會摧毀我們的專注能力。

那該怎麼解決呢?

第一,創造一個能讓你不受干擾工作的環境。把手機關掉。如果你有獨立辦公室,就把門關上。如果你在隔間裡工作,讓同事知道你希望在某段時間內不被打擾。如果你在家工作,有人敲門就別理會。

第二,以時間區塊(time chunks)的方式工作。工作 30 分鐘、休息 5 分鐘;或是工作 50 分鐘、休息 10 分鐘,由你自己決定工作與休息時段的長度。

第三,堅持單工作業。每個時間區塊只做一件事,不多做。

就是這樣。做到這三件事,你就能減少注意力殘留帶來的困擾。想想看,當你終於能夠專心時,你的生產力會提升多少!

下次,我會分享一個能讓你更能掌控一天行程的簡單技巧。它可能不容易做到,但絕對有效。

敬請期待,祝你有美好的一週!

emails.subject: Calgon, take me away...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I used to think working long hours without breaks was the best way to get stuff done. After all, with so much to do, who has time to take breaks?

Boy, was I wrong.

It turns out that taking breaks increases productivity. And not taking them lessens it.

Science backs me up on this.

A few years back, DeskTime, a time-tracking service, looked at data about workers' behavior. The researchers found something interesting. The employees who got the most done didn't work for hours on end without breaks. Not even close. They worked for 52 minutes and then took a 17-minute break.

Bunch of lazy bums! But the data showed those lazy bums were killing it in terms of productivity.

In 2009, the journal Research in Occupational Stress and Well Being published a study examining the effects of taking breaks. The authors noted:

"For each of the different types of work breaks studied, we can generally conclude that activities that removed or reduced demands, work related or otherwise, tended to result in more positive outcomes."

That's a fancy way of saying taking breaks led to better work.

Don't take my word for it. And don't rely on the scientists' findings. Try it yourself. Organize your day into time chunks with set durations for your work sessions and breaks. For example:

- work for 25 minutes and take a 5-minute break
- work for 45 minutes and take a 10-minute break
- work for 60 minutes and take a 15-minute break

Or follow the lead of the employees in the DeskTime study. Work for 52 minutes and take a 17-minute break.

If you can take breaks and get more done, why on earth would you want to work nonstop for hours on end? I know I wouldn't!

If you're not familiar with using time chunks as a productivity tool, now's the time to learn about it.

Talk to you in a week or so,

Damon Zahariades
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

我以前一直認為,長時間不休息地工作才是把事情做完的最佳方式。畢竟事情這麼多,誰還有時間休息?

天哪,我大錯特錯。

事實證明,適時休息反而能提升生產力,而不休息則會降低生產力。

科學研究也支持我這個說法。

幾年前,時間追蹤服務 DeskTime 分析了員工行為的資料,研究人員發現了一件有趣的事:完成最多工作的員工,並不是那些連續工作好幾個小時不休息的人,完全不是。他們是工作 52 分鐘、然後休息 17 分鐘的人。

一群懶惰蟲!但數據顯示,這些「懶惰蟲」在生產力上表現得非常出色。

2009 年,期刊《Research in Occupational Stress and Well Being》發表了一項探討休息影響的研究。作者指出:

「在我們研究的各種工作休息類型中,我們大致可以得出結論:那些能夠移除或減少工作(或其他)要求的活動,往往能帶來更正面的結果。」

用白話來說,就是休息能帶來更好的工作成果。

別只聽我說,也別只依賴科學家的研究結果,親自試試看吧。把你的一天安排成一個個「時間區塊」,為工作時段和休息時段設定固定的長度。例如:

- 工作 25 分鐘,休息 5 分鐘
- 工作 45 分鐘,休息 10 分鐘
- 工作 60 分鐘,休息 15 分鐘

或者你也可以仿效 DeskTime 研究中的那些員工,工作 52 分鐘、休息 17 分鐘。

如果休息反而能讓你完成更多事,那你到底為什麼要不停工作好幾個小時呢?反正我是不會這麼做的!

如果你還不熟悉如何運用時間區塊來提升生產力,現在正是學習的好時機。

大約一週後再聊,

emails.subject: Be your own measuring stick...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

My friend Brian and I have an ongoing joke. Here's the backstory...

Brian isn't exactly what you'd call detail-oriented. More things fall through the cracks than don't with him.

He admits it. Heck, he's even proud of it. He wears it like a badge of honor.

When tasks go unfinished or files get lost, he'll grin and say things like "I'm a big picture kind of guy" or "Details? We pay other people to worry about details."

But it never fails. Every single performance review he receives from his bosses makes the same claim: Brian's a detail-oriented employee.

Of course, he can't wait to share this with me. "See?" he says. "I'm great with details! It says so right here!" And then we laugh about how his bosses must be tipping a few back just to get through his performance reviews.

But there's a lesson to be found here: other people are terrible gauges of your productivity.

Don't trust them. Set reasonable goals for whatever you need to get done. Then, measure your progress according to those goals.

In other words, be your own measuring stick.

I've been told, "I can't believe how much you manage to write." But if I'm being honest, I could boost my output by three-fold.

That's why I don't rely on others to gauge my productivity. It's not their fault. They just don't know me as well as I do.

Think about this as it relates to your own life the next time someone applauds how much you get done. Do they truly know what you're capable of? Can you do better?

If you want to take your productivity to the next level, make sure you're not doing any of these 30 bad habits.

Talk soon!

Damon Zahariades

emails.subject: How I avoid distracting thoughts...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I hate distractions.

They're a double whammy on my productivity. They break my momentum, which is bad enough. But each time that happens, I need 20 minutes to get back on track!

I'll bet you can relate.

For me, the worst type of distraction is self-induced. I'm always thinking of things I need to do, even while I'm working on other stuff.

Here's an example: I recently sat down to write my next book. Here are the thoughts that went through my head...

- I need to order a cover for the book
- Ideas for new books, blogs, emails
- Review the paperback edition of To-Do List Formula
- Make a reservation for dinner on Friday
- Check my email
- Do I have enough meat in the freezer?
- Call my parents and schedule a lunch date
- I should call my friend Jeremy for coffee
- I need to get together with my buddy Dan
- Review my ads on Amazon
- When do my domain names expire?
- I wonder what's happening on Facebook?

There was so much stuff floating through my noggin' that I couldn't concentrate on writing my book!

Here's how I solved the problem...

I wrote down every thought onto a "tiny tasks" list. It was like playing Whack-A-Mole. Each time a thought surfaced, I'd whack it by writing it down.

The result? Instant relief.

I was able to focus, confident that I wouldn't forget to do something that needed to get done. After all, every thought was now on a list I could review at my leisure.

With that out of the way, I got on with writing my book. It was a very productive session!

If delinquent thoughts distract you, write 'em down and get back to work. You'll be able to better focus on the task at hand.

By the way, a "tiny tasks" list is a small cog in a much larger system. If you'd like to create an effective to-do list system for yourself, one that actually works, here's the blueprint.

We'll talk soon!

Damon Zahariades

emails.subject: Are You Using An Ignore List? Here's Why You Should And How To Do It
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

You won't find a bigger advocate of using to-do lists than me. Heck, I wrote an entire book on the topic! To-do lists are one of the main reasons I'm able to keep multiple projects moving forward.

Having said that, there's another list you should review each morning before you start your day: your ignore list.

What's an ignore list?

It's a list of everything that might distract you from getting things done. Here's part of my ignore list:

- Facebook
- KBoards forum
- news websites
- email
- my phone
- the front door

I keep it on my desk while I work. But frankly, it's become unnecessary. I've trained myself to ignore these items over the years, so I rarely look at my list anymore.

But if you've never taken the time to write down your biggest distractions, I strongly encourage you to do so. It only takes a minute.

The upside?

You'll feel more focused after reviewing your list each morning.

You'll be more "plugged in" to the day's most important tasks and projects.

And best of all, you'll be less likely to give in to the temptations of Facebook and other distractions.

That's it. Short and sweet.

We'll talk soon!

Damon Zahariades

P.S. If you're having trouble getting through your daily to-do lists, check out my book To-Do List Formula: A Stress-Free Guide To Creating To-Do Lists That Work!

emails.subject: 23 of my best email productivity tips
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I recently cleaned out one of my old Gmail inboxes (I have several). It contained more than 24,000 emails. It took me three hours to organize everything, but I finally got it done.

While getting things organized, I couldn't help but think about my process for managing emails. I've got it down to a science. As a result, I save myself a ton of time.

You might benefit from learning how I do things. So below, you'll find my top 23 email productivity tips.

Most of them are extremely simple. That's good news because it means you can start using them right now. Fair warning: I'm going to go through them quickly to keep this email as concise as possible.

1. Check your email twice a day. Once in the morning and once at night. No more. (By the way, this is the first crucial habit I cover in The 30-Day Productivity Plan.)
2. Limit each inbox session to 15 minutes.
3. Keep your emails short. Short emails encourage short responses.
4. Indicate your desired actions in your subject lines.
5. Don't respond to emails that don't require responses.
6. Think twice before sending emails. Remember, the less you send, the less you get in return.
7. Don't cc people just to keep them "in the loop."
8. Let emails age before you respond. Set expectations.
9. Set up filters to tag and archive "daily deal" emails.
10. Unsubscribe from most newsletters (not this one, of course!)
11. Create form letter emails for responses you send over and over.
12. Limit each email you send to a single topic or idea.
13. Set up a folder system that makes sense to you. For example, create separate folders for "Personal Email," "Work Email," "Newsletters," "Daily Deals," etc.
14. Set up a "Reply By [Date]" folder. Archive emails that require a response, but not an immediate one.
15. Don't let emails sit in your inbox. Either take action on them, archive them, delegate them, or delete them.
16. Use the Touch-It-Once principle. Read emails once and decide what to do them immediately afterwards.
17. Use the 2-Minute Rule from David Allen's Getting It Done (GTD) system. Most emails can be handled in two minutes or less.
18. Use the phone instead of email to avoid a back-and-forth thread.
19. Turn off Facebook and Twitter email notifications.
20. Learn to use keyboard shortcuts. For example, with Gmail, "e" archives selected messages, "c" allows you to compose a new message, and "r" allows you to reply to the sender.
21. Don't stress out about getting to "Inbox Zero." It's unnecessary. The tips we're covering will get you 95% of the way there. That's good enough.
22. Don't worry about setting up dozens of folders. Set up a few according to context ("personal," "work," etc.). You can always use your email app's search function to find what you need.
23. Close your email application when you're not using it.

That's it. These 23 email productivity "hacks" will streamline how you handle your email and save you a ton of time in the process.

If you're using a hack that I've missed, hit reply. I'd love to hear about it!

Let's talk soon,
Damon Zahariades

P.S. I'm thinking about writing an action guide explaining everything I know related to email productivity. If that's something you're interested in, hit reply and let me know!
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

我最近清理了我其中一個舊的 Gmail 信箱(我有好幾個)。裡面有超過 24,000 封郵件,花了我三個小時才整理完,不過總算搞定了。

整理的過程中,我不禁思考起自己管理郵件的方法。老實說,我已經把這件事變成一門精確的科學,因此為自己省下了大量時間。

你或許也能從我的做法中受益,所以以下是我最推薦的 23 個電子郵件生產力技巧。

大部分都非常簡單,這是好消息,因為代表你現在就能開始使用。先說一聲:為了讓這封信盡量簡潔,我會很快地把每一條都過一遍。

1. 每天只檢查兩次郵件,早上一次、晚上一次,不要更多。(順帶一提,這是我在《The 30-Day Productivity Plan》中提到的第一個重要習慣。)
2. 每次查看信箱的時間限制在 15 分鐘內。
3. 讓你的郵件保持簡短。簡短的郵件會鼓勵對方也給出簡短的回覆。
4. 在主旨欄裡就清楚標明你希望對方採取的行動。
5. 不需要回覆的郵件就不要回。
6. 寄出郵件前多想一下。記住,你寄得越少,收到的回覆也會越少。
7. 不要只是為了讓別人「知道一下」就把他們加進副本。
8. 讓郵件先擱置一段時間再回覆,設立好對方的期待。
9. 設定篩選規則,自動標記並歸檔「每日優惠」類的郵件。
10. 取消訂閱大部分電子報(當然,這一份不算在內!)
11. 針對經常需要重複回覆的內容,建立制式回覆範本。
12. 每封信只談一個主題或一個想法。
13. 建立一套對你來說合理的資料夾系統。例如分別建立「私人郵件」「工作郵件」「電子報」「每日優惠」等資料夾。
14. 建立一個「[日期]前回覆」資料夾,用來歸檔那些需要回覆、但不急著馬上回的郵件。
15. 不要讓郵件一直躺在收件匣裡。要嘛立刻處理,要嘛歸檔、轉交他人或直接刪除。
16. 採用「一次觸碰原則」(Touch-It-Once):讀一次郵件後就立刻決定該怎麼處理。
17. 運用 David Allen 的 GTD(Getting Things Done)系統中的「兩分鐘原則」:大多數郵件都能在兩分鐘或更短時間內處理完畢。
18. 遇到需要來回討論的事情,改用電話溝通,避免沒完沒了的郵件串。
19. 關閉 Facebook 和 Twitter 的郵件通知。
20. 學會使用快捷鍵。例如在 Gmail 中,按「e」可以歸檔選取的郵件、按「c」可以撰寫新郵件、按「r」可以回覆寄件者。
21. 不要為了達到「收件匣清空」而給自己壓力,那並非必要。我們談到的這些技巧就能讓你達成 95% 的效果,這已經很足夠了。
22. 不用擔心要設立幾十個資料夾,依照情境(如「私人」「工作」等)建立幾個就好,你隨時都可以用信箱的搜尋功能找到需要的東西。
23. 不使用電子郵件應用程式時就把它關閉。

就是這樣。這 23 個電子郵件生產力「小撇步」能讓你處理郵件的方式更加流暢,並為你省下大量時間。

如果你正在用一個我沒提到的技巧,歡迎直接回信告訴我,我很想聽聽看!

改天聊,
戴蒙・查哈里亞德斯

emails.subject: Are you using the 2-minute rule?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Ever heard of the 2-minute rule? It's a great way to overcome procrastination. Here's how it works:

If you can get something done in less than two minutes, do it right now. Don't wait. Don't put it off. Just do it.

It's as simple as that.

Here are five quick ways you can use this rule during your day...

* while reviewing your to-do list (what can you get done right now?)
* while checking your email (can you write a response in less than two minutes?)
* when developing a new habit (want to start doing pushups? Drop and give me 10!)
* to de-stress (close your eyes, take a few deep breaths, and relax)
* to clear off your desk (remove items that are cluttering your workspace)

That's just the tip of the iceberg. There are tons of applications for the 2-minute rule. The best part is that you can start using it right now.

This tactic was introduced by David Allen, who created the "Getting Things Done" (GTD) system. I'm not a huge fan of GTD, but I absolutely love the 2-minute rule. (I've created a more focused to-do list system, which I describe in detail in my book To-Do List Formula: A Stress-Free Guide To Creating To-Do Lists That Work!)

If you're struggling with procrastination, give the 2-minute rule a try. You'll be amazed at how many small to-do items you'll be able to cross off your list.

Talk soon,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. Remember, sharing is caring. Share these tips with a friend and help him or her to be more productive!

emails.subject: 5 simple ways you can make the most of your spare minutes
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Let me ask you a question.

Do you make the most of your "in between" time? I'm referring to the spare minutes you have between activities.

For example, suppose you're waiting for a client to call. What do you with the 10 to 15 minutes beforehand.

Or suppose you're waiting for the New England Patriots game to start.

Or let's say you're at the dentist's office waiting for your appointment.

Are you productive during those minutes or do you squander them by checking social media, playing games, and reading the latest news headlines?

We waste a lot of time each day by letting spare minutes slip through our fingers. We can do better. A lot better.

Here are 5 things you can do to make the most of your "in between" time.

#1 - Watch a TED talk.
If you have 20 minutes to spare, go to TED.com and find a talk on a subject that interests you. I recently watched Tony Robbins's talk "Why We Do What We Do" and Shawn Anchor's "The Happy Secret To Better Work." Both were fun, engaging, and insightful.

#2 - Plan your tomorrow.
Create a list of to-do items and schedule time for them on your calendar. This is also a good time to review tomorrow's schedule and make adjustments as needed.

#3 - Learn how to do something.
Five spare minutes gives you an opportunity to broaden your skill set. Head over to KhanAcademy.org or YouTube and find an educational video. I recently watched Gordon Ramsey's video on how to slow-cook beef short ribs on YouTube. It was five minutes long and taught me the basics.

#4 - Declutter your phone.
You probably have apps you no longer use. Delete them to free up space and speed up your phone. Keep your home screen clutter-free and tidy! (When you have time, make this step a part of a Digital Detox!)

#5 - Work those arms and abs.
Don't wait until you have an hour to spend at the gym. If you have in-between time, drop and give me 10! Push-ups, situps, crunches, and lunges can be done in minutes. As a bonus, you'll enjoy a quick surge of energy.

You can be productive while waiting for other things to happen. Instead of compulsively checking email or social media during your spare minutes, try the five ideas above.

Make the most of your downtime!

Talk soon,

Damon Zahariades

emails.subject: An amazing story about grit
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

I've been thinking a lot about grit lately.

Not the bits of sand you find between your toes after spending a day at the beach. I'm talking about the ability to persevere toward a goal no matter what obstacles are in your way.

A few days ago, I was reading about a man named Yusai Sakai. He was known as the marathon monk. When you hear his story, you'll appreciate the idea of grit.

Here's the short version...

Sakai was a Buddhist monk who worshipped in a temple on Mount Hiei, located just north of Kyoto in Japan. He was a member of the Tendai Buddhist monks, a group that seeks enlightenment in a variety of ways.

The toughest is something called the Sennichi Kaihogyo.

The Sennichi Kaihogyo is a 1,000-day trek. The 1,000 days are broken into 100-day segments, which are completed over seven years. The distances walked by the monks increase each year. By year 7, they're walking over 50 miles a day.

If you had the same reaction as I did, your jaw just dropped.

But wait... there's more.

If any monk undertaking the Sennichi Kaihogyo fails to complete a day's journey, there are consequences. And by consequences, I don't mean he's berated by the head monk or forced to go without dinner.

No. He's expected to commit suicide.

I imagine your jaw just dropped again. Mine sure did when I read that.

Back to Yusai Sakai.

This amazing man not only completed the Sennichi Kaihogyo (a feat in and of itself), but managed to do so TWICE. Sakai is one of only three monks who hold that distinction.

And here's the kicker...

He was 61 years old when he completed it the second time.

He'd wake up at midnight and finish the day's walking at 9:00 p.m. Then, he'd do it again the next day. And the day after that. And over and over until he completed the trek.

Now, THAT'S grit.

Sakai passed away in 2013 at age 87. But the lessons he taught by example will inspire people for years to come.

Did his story inspire you? Click the reply button and let me know.

Damon Zahariades

P.S. It takes a fair amount of grit to commit yourself to making the most of your time. If you're facing obstacles, pick up a copy of my book The 30-Day Productivity Plan: Break The 30 Bad Habits That Are Sabotaging Your Time Management - One Day At A Time! You're bound to find the solution.
emails.contentZh:
嗨 張振輝,

我最近一直在思考「毅力」(grit)這件事。

不是海邊玩一整天後夾在腳趾間的那種沙粒,我說的是無論遇到什麼阻礙,都能堅持朝目標邁進的能力。

簡短版是這樣的……

酒井是一位在日本京都北方比叡山上一座寺廟修行的佛教僧侶。他屬於天台宗僧團,這個團體以各種方式追求開悟。

其中最艱難的修行叫做「千日回峰行」。

千日回峰行是一趟為期1,000天的徒步修行。這1,000天被分成以100天為一段的區間,總共歷時七年完成。僧侶每年行走的距離都會增加,到第七年時,他們每天要走超過50英里。

如果你的反應跟我一樣,現在應該下巴都要掉下來了。

但等等……還沒完。

如果進行千日回峰行的僧侶未能完成當天的行程,是有後果的。而這個後果,可不是被住持責罵或不准吃晚飯那麼簡單。

不,他被要求切腹自盡。

我猜你的下巴又掉下來了一次。我讀到這裡時確實也是如此。

回到酒井雄哉的故事。

這位了不起的人物不僅完成了千日回峰行(光是這樣就已經是壯舉),而且還完成了「兩次」。酒井是僅有的三位擁有此殊榮的僧侶之一。

更厲害的是……

他第二次完成時已經61歲了。

他每天半夜起床,一路走到晚上9點才結束當天的行程。然後隔天再來一次,再隔天又一次,如此反覆直到完成整趟修行。

這,才叫毅力。

酒井在2013年以87歲高齡辭世,但他以身作則所傳授的道理,將持續激勵人們許多年。

他的故事有激勵到你嗎?點擊回覆讓我知道。

Damon Zahariades

emails.subject: Do this if you're feeling burnt out
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Last time, I showed you seven ways to tell whether you're overcommitted and on the verge of burnout. If you need to refresh your memory, read the article on the AOP blog.

Today, I'm give you a quick and simple plan to remedy that situation. If you're feeling exhausted, overwhelmed and stressed, I recommend you do the following:

#1 - Cancel non-critical appointments and purge non-critical to-do items from your calendar.
You need time to rest. This is the quickest, simplest way to acquire it.

#2 - Start saying "no."
Fair warning: people are going to be disappointed. That's their problem, not yours. Say "no" and reclaim your time.

#3 - Choose a hobby.
Whether it's gardening, playing basketball or reading mystery novels, pick one and do it with the extra time you've given yourself. If you don't fill that free time, others will try to fill it for you.

#4 - Figure out the "why."
You're feeling overwhelmed and frustrated for a reason. Identify it. Keep a "stress journal" if you have to.

#5 - Address the triggers.
Once you know the root causes of your stress, you can make positive changes. That might mean hiring an assistant, taking weekends off or getting more sleep.

#6 - Reevaluate whether you're still working toward your goals.
It's easy to get off track. If you're spending time on things that aren't moving you closer to your goals, stop. Reassess. Realign yourself.

#7 - Commit to avoiding unnecessary stress.
If you don't commit, the changes you make won't last. They'll be short-lived and you'll find yourself dealing with overwhelm again in the future.

We'll talk about the theory of stress and overcommitment later. For now, it's more important that you take action. Theory is great when we're talking about prevention. But it isn't worth much if you're already on the edge of burnout.

If you devote yourself to doing the seven things I've suggested above, I guarantee you'll regain the passion you once felt for your work.

Talk to you soon,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. Be sure to pick up a copy of my book The 30-Day Productivity Plan: Break The 30 Bad Habits That Are Sabotaging Your Time Management - One Day At A Time! Discover how you might be unintentionally wrecking your own productivity.

emails.subject: Do you have a power hour?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

You know what it's like.

You have a to-do list filled with small tasks that never seem to go away.

They nag you. They harass you. They remind you that you're neglecting your responsibilities.

Worse, they don't have deadlines. So instead of tackling them and crossing them off your to-do list, you carry them forward day after day.

And there they sit, every day, badgering you to give them attention.

I get it. I relate. There are tasks on my to-do list that I truly dislike. One example is vacuuming the floors in my house. It's not difficult. It's not even that time-consuming. It's just dull.

So, rather than rolling up my sleeves and actually doing the chore, I carry it forward.

And I chide myself every... single... time.

But recently, I've been using a tactic to "short circuit" this bad habit. I call it my Power Hour (I didn't come up with the name).

What is my Power Hour? It's a 60-minute time block devoted to addressing all of the tasks I've been procrastinating on. Here are a few examples:

* doing laundry
* visiting the grocery store
* reconciling my checking account
* reviewing my Amazon sales reports
* calling my parents
* paying bills

You get the picture. And I'll bet you can relate to what I'm talking about.

Maybe you've been wanting to plan a vacation, but haven't been motivated to buy plane tickets or reserve a hotel room.

Perhaps you've been meaning to call your friend with the phone number to your dentist, but haven't gotten around to it.

Or maybe you've been neglecting your garden and know it needs a little tender loving care.

Here's my question for you: do you have a power hour to handle these small tasks?

If not, I recommend giving it a try. Set aside 60 minutes, grab your master to-do list and knock out those small items that nag you for attention each and every day.

You may be surprised at how productive you are during that hour.

I'd be willing to bet you'll make a huge dent in your to-do list. Imagine how good it will feel as you cross out item after item!

One hour. That's all it takes.

Give it a try and let me know how it goes!

Until next time,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. If you're having trouble getting through your daily to-do lists, you're probably using the wrong approach. But there's a simple solution. Check out my book To-Do List Formula: A Stress-Free Guide To Creating To-Do Lists That Work! to learn how to create an effective to-do list system.

P.P.S. If you think one of your friends or family members might benefit from these emails, encourage him or her to sign up at this link. Why not enjoy a boost of productivity with someone you love?

emails.subject: 8 morning rituals
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Ever gotten a late start and had trouble catching up?

I've written a new blog post that offers a solution. I think you'll like it. It's titled "8 Morning Rituals to Kick Off a Successful Day."

Your morning sets the tone for your entire day. That's the way we're built. And that's why many of the most successful people in the world maintain small morning rituals.

Doing so helps them to focus. It alleviates stress. And it helps them to get their priorities straight.

Want some examples? Try these on for size:

1. Entrepreneur Gary Vaynerchuk spends 3 hours each morning catching up on business news and connecting with key people in his organization. It's part of his ritual.

2. Dilbert creator Scott Adams spends the first 20 minutes of his day eating a protein bar and sipping a hot cup of coffee. Sounds simple, right? But he notes "I want to train myself to enjoy waking up and being productive. It totally works."

3. NFL Hall-of-Fame inductee Fran Tarkenton spends his morning reading different sections of the newspaper, even the ones that bore him. He says, "Sticking to a routine has always brought me clarity of thought, a positive mindset, and most of all, successful results for the rest of the day."

4. Kevin O'Leary, the bad boy investor of Shark Tank, spends his mornings keeping a close eye on the international bond markets. Then, he works out for 45 minutes. He says "Your health is one investment that is guaranteed to pay dividends!"

5. Arianna Huffington, creator of The Huffington Post, does yoga and meditates. She says "it helps set my intention for the day."

If these 5 power players think morning rituals are a good idea, it's definitely worth looking into.

I wrote the latest blog post to give you several ideas (8 in total) to get you started.

Click here to read it on AOP. You're going to love it! :)

Let's talk soon,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. If you enjoyed this email, forward it to a friend. Let him or her know how to join my newsletter and grab my free book Catapult Your Productivity: The Top 10 Habits You Must Develop To Get More Things Done.

emails.subject: Here's a quick 'n dirty productivity hack...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Remember last week when we talked about beating procrastination? I gave you several tips on how to do it.

Today, I'd like to share a simple formula that might help you win the battle once and for all. There's a small bit of math involved.

But don't worry. It's quick and painless. :)

Here's the formula:

(10+2)*5

A man named Merlin Mann came up with it. If you don't know Merlin, he's the guy who created the now-defunct blog 43Folders.

The formula is a procrastination hack. It's designed to spur you to get to work when you're distracted.

Here's how it works:

Step 1: Work on a task for 10 minutes.

Step 2: Then, take a 2-minute break.

Step 3: Do that 4 more times.

By the end, you'll have spent an hour. And hopefully, you'll have completed a bunch of small tasks sitting on your to-do list.

Don't feel like you have to complete the task you're working on during a 10-minute work session. That's not important. The important thing is that you're focused on it.

That's the beauty of the formula. Merlin figured anybody could hunker down and work without getting distracted for 10 minutes. Facebook will be there waiting for you on your 2-minute break.

If you're thinking Merlin's formula sounds a lot like the Pomodoro Technique, you're right! Great catch. Just goes to show that it works.

One last note: use a timer. I prefer to use one of those noisy kitchen timers that shrieks like a banshee when the time is up. You might prefer to use your phone.

Either option is fine. Different strokes for different folks.

Let's stop here. If you're constantly distracted at work or you're a habitual procrastinator, give Merlin's formula a try. I'll bet it'll help.

If you DO try it, shoot me an email and let me know how it went!

Talk to you soon,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. Forward this on to a friend or family member who might find it useful. Be a hero to that person. While you're at it, encourage them to sign up for this newsletter!

公式是這樣的:

這是一位名叫 Merlin Mann 的人提出的。如果你不認識 Merlin,他就是創立了那個現已停止更新的部落格「43Folders」的人。

這個公式是一種對抗拖延的小技巧,目的是在你分心時,推動你重新投入工作。

運作方式如下:

第一步:專注做一項任務10分鐘。

emails.subject: Here's how to beat procrastination
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Are you sick of procrastinating?

I can relate. Believe me.

Procrastination is the great equalizer. Everyone does it. You. Me. Even the guy next door who seems to have it all together.

Hell, I'm sure even Sir Richard Branson, a go-getter who runs more than 300 companies, does it on occasion.

Today, I'm going to give you a single tip for beating it.

Before we get to that tip, let's be clear about something. The habit of putting things off until later is psychological. So it's important to have the right expectations when you're trying to tame that beast of a bad habit.

The tip I'm about to give you is just a starting point. It's not a magical elixir that will fix the problem for the rest of your days.

If you're been procrastinating your entire life, you need a complete guide to getting that beast under control. That means learning about the psychology of procrastination and hitting it hard at the source.

I'm writing that guide right now. In the meantime, my book The 30-Day Productivity Plan: Break The 30 Bad Habits That Are Sabotaging Your Time Management - One Day At A Time! covers procrastination on Day 10. It also provides several actionable tips for controlling the urge to put things off. Grab a copy at Amazon for less than you'd spend on a caffè latte.

Anyway, here's today's tip for beating procrastination...

Revisit the reasons you want to - or need to - get a certain task done.

Let me give you a personal example.

I'm in the middle of writing a new book (not the procrastination-beating guide). The problem is, I've been lacking in the motivation department.

Surprise, surprise, my progress on the book has slowed to a snail's pace.

So last week, I sat down at my local Starbucks and reviewed some of my personal reasons for writing the book.

Here they are:

- help people deal with a common problem that limits their output
- boost my reputation as a productivity expert
- attract new readers for my books
- introduce more folks to my blog
- encourage more people to subscribe to my email newsletter about productivity
- generate another income stream
- add to my growing catalog of actionable guides for getting more done

That did the trick! Reminding myself of those reasons gave me a huge burst of motivation to finish writing the book.

And now, I'm almost finished with the first draft.

See how that works?

Here's what I want you to do...

Identify one task that you're unmotivated to complete. Sit down and list all of the reasons you want to complete it.

It's a great way to rediscover your motivation, which will spur you toward getting that task done. Or you might find that there's no reason to work on it anymore. If that's the case, chuck it.

Either way, you win!

I'm putting together a blog post on the subject that you'll definitely want to read. I'll let you know when it's finished.

Let's talk in a few days.

Damon Zahariades

P.S. If you use the tip above, let me know how it works out for you. Send me an email telling me whether you got a burst of motivation that helped you to banish the procrastination monster.

emails.subject: The 10 biggest productivity killers...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

It's Damon from ArtOfProductivity.com.

Last time we talked, I told you that we're going to cover the top 10 productivity killers.

Let's do that today.

These are the 10 things that will prevent you from getting things done and enjoying a rewarding life. They're nasty little buggers because they sneak into your day and become bad habits.

And like any bad habit, they're hard to break.

If you notice any of the following in your daily workflow, you need to route them out. Your productivity depends on it!

Enough specious claptrap. Here they are:

1. Email
2. Phone calls
3. Text messages
4. Social media
5. Internet surfing
6. Being a perfectionist
7. News
8. Noisy environment
9. Talking with coworkers
10. Procrastination

Each one, on its own, can destroy your momentum when you're trying to finish a project. Each one can derail your efforts and totally sabotage your goals for the day (or week!)

I've written about ways to overcome some of those productivity killers on my blog. So check out the archives. If you can't find something, just give me a shout.

At this point, you might be thinking, "Wait a second Damon. There are only 10 things to worry about?!"

Nope. There are actually more than 100.

But the ones listed above are the most common. They're the things everyone seems to deal with while trying to get stuff done.

We'll explore some neat hacks for beating these buggers in future emails.

For now, read through that list again. Identify the items that are acting like an anchor on your productivity. Then, take steps to eliminate them from your day.

Next time, I'll give you a few tips for beating procrastination. You're going to want to read that email. Apply the tips I give you and watch your output soar!

Damon Zahariades

P.S. Need a simple workflow system to manage your time better throughout the day? Try the Time Chunking Method. I wrote a book on it that covers much more than the basics you'll find online. Click here to see what's inside the book and to grab a copy. It costs less than a value meal at McDonalds.

6. 完美主義

emails.subject: 張振輝, how effective are your "to do" lists?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Damon here.

Over the past few weeks, we've talked about strategies you can use to gain control of your day and squeeze more productivity from your daily workflow.

By now, I hope you've seen some improvement - even gradual improvement - in your output. If not, let me know where you're facing challenges and I'll try to help.

In the meantime, let's talk about your to-do lists.

There's a good chance you're doing them wrong. I know I was. And it prevented me from getting through the items listed on them.

Tell me if this sounds familiar...

You start the day with a ton of items on your list. You've had your caffeine and are optimistic about getting through them.

So you get to work.

Throughout the day, more items get added to the list. Each item you cross off is replaced by two others. By the time you're ready to call it a day, your list has more items on it than you started with.

Talk about discouraging!

I know you can relate.

Here's a little tip: simplify your to-do lists.

Don't overcrowd them with non-critical items. If there's a task that needs to be completed at some point in the future, but not today, put it on a master to-do list. Your DAILY to-do list should include no more than 10 items, and preferably 5.

Give it a try.

If you'd like to learn how to create a complete to-do list system, grab a copy of my book To-Do List Formula: A Stress-Free Guide To Creating To-Do Lists That Work!

In the meantime, starting tomorrow, create a list of items that need to get done by the end of the day. Don't add anything to your list unless you absolutely have to.

Then, focus on getting through those must-do items. Cross them off as you complete them. You'll stand a much better chance of ending your day with every item on your list crossed out.

And let me tell you, it's an awesome feeling! It'll motivate you to do the same thing the following day.

Believe it or not, there's an art to creating effective to-do lists. I show you the basics in Catapult Your Productivity!, the ebook you downloaded when you subscribed. If you haven't read that section of the book, now's the time to do so.

You'll find it under Habit #5 on pages 15 through 18.

As a heads-up, I've got a ton of great stuff for you in the coming days. Definitely stay tuned.

Until next time,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. I'm putting together a battle plan for the blog based on what you've told me are your greatest productivity challenges. You're going to love what I have in store for you.

emails.subject: Answers to your questions about time tracking...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

It's Damon from ArtOfProductivity.com.

Do you remember when I mentioned a couple weeks ago that you should be tracking your time?

A lot of folks have since emailed me about that. They want to know how I do it and how they can make the best use of the data.

Let's cover that right now. I'll cover some of the questions I've received in a Q&A format below.

"Damon, what are you using to track your time?"

I use an old-fashioned kitchen timer. Then, I put the numbers into a spreadsheet. That way, I can sort the data in any fashion I choose.

It works for me, but it may not for you. I've also used Toggl.com. It's a great app because it's simple, works in your browser and you can create pretty reports with it. Also, it's free.

Although I really like Toggl, I ended up going back to my kitchen timer and spreadsheet just because I'm accustomed to using them. It's a dumb reason, I admit. But there you have it.

I just signed up for FreshBooks, which has a time tracker built into the platform. I'm going to try it one of these days and report back.

"What are the best time-tracking apps out there?"

Besides Toggl, I've heard good things about RescueTime, Chrometa, Freckle, Hours and ATracker. Frankly, there are hundreds of time trackers out there and I don't want to spend the time learning how to use them all.

My needs are pretty basic. I just need to know how long it takes me to do certain tasks and what percentage of my day and week is spent doing them.

My kitchen timer and spreadsheet do that for me.

One of the downsides to following the latest and greatest time tracking apps is that they'll be outdated when next year's crop comes out. Trying to keep up with the latest and greatest is a never-ending battle.

Having said that, I cover the apps I like best on my blog.

Click to read "Top 6 Time-Tracking Apps To Boost Your Productivity."

Just remember, the list of apps in that blog post is nowhere close to being a complete list.

"Damon, how do I use my numbers to increase my productivity?"

That's a great question. Data isn't worth anything unless you put it to use.

I'll explain what I do. You may be able to apply it directly to your own process. Or you might need to tweak it a little. At the very least, it's a starting point.

One of the items I track is how long it takes me to write blog posts. Suppose over a month, I figure out that it takes me 2 hours. That includes researching, writing, editing and posting the material, along with finding a good image to accompany it.

So I have my data. Now what?

First, I like to challenge myself. So I'm going to try to write blog posts in 1 hour and 55 minutes. If I can do so consistently, I'll use that as a new benchmark and try to write blog posts in 1 hour and 50 minutes.

You get the idea.

Second, I use the data as a deadline.

Instead of letting my timer count up while I write my blog post, I set it for 2 hours and let it count down. The timer sits in front of me where I can see the seconds and minutes tick by.

That's motivating to me. If I'm behind schedule, I pick up the pace to make sure I meet my deadline.

The third thing I do with the data is track how I'm spending my time throughout the week.

I like to keep a bird's-eye view of my output. If I'm spending 70% of my writing time on the blog, it means I'm not devoting enough time to writing Kindle books and other information products.

Can you apply your numbers in the same way? That depends on how you work and the goals you're working toward. But now you know how I do it.

Let's close this out since this email is already too long. I have a lot more to say about time tracking, but it can wait until later.

For now, here's the most important tip I can give you on this topic: start tracking your time today. Don't wait. Start building the habit right now.

And if you must use an online app to do it, be sure to check out my blog where I cover the top 5 (in my opinion).

Here's the link again: Top 6 Time-Tracking Apps To Boost Your Productivity

If you end up using any of the apps mentioned in that blog post, let me know what you think of them.

The good, bad, and the ugly.

Either way, I'll talk to you again in a few days.

Until then,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. Remember to tell me what you're struggling with when it comes to increasing your productivity.

嘿 張振輝,

我是ArtOfProductivity.com的Damon。

還記得幾週前我提到你應該要追蹤自己的時間嗎?

之後有很多人寫信問我這件事,他們想知道我是怎麼做的,以及如何善用這些數據。

現在就來談談這個。我會用問答的形式,回答一些我收到的問題。

「Damon,你用什麼工具來追蹤時間?」

我用一個老派的廚房計時器,然後把數字輸入到試算表裡。這樣我就能用任何方式排序這些數據。

這對我有效,但對你來說可能不適用。我也用過Toggl.com,這是一款很棒的應用程式,因為它簡單易用,可以在瀏覽器中運作,還能製作漂亮的報表。而且是免費的。

雖然我真的很喜歡Toggl,但最後還是回去用廚房計時器和試算表,單純只是因為我已經習慣了。我承認這理由挺蠢的,但事實就是如此。

我剛註冊了FreshBooks,這個平台內建了時間追蹤器。改天我會試試看,再跟你回報。

「市面上最好的時間追蹤應用程式是哪些?」

除了Toggl之外,我還聽說RescueTime、Chrometa、Freckle、Hours和ATracker都不錯。老實說,市面上有數百種時間追蹤工具,我不想花時間全部學會怎麼用。

我的需求其實很基本。我只需要知道完成某些任務要花多少時間,以及這些任務佔了我一天和一週多少比例的時間。

我的廚房計時器和試算表就能幫我做到這一點。

追逐最新最好的時間追蹤應用程式的缺點之一,就是明年又會出新的一批,讓它們變得過時。想跟上最新最好的東西,是一場永無止境的戰鬥。

話雖如此,我在部落格上分享了我最喜歡的一些應用程式。

點擊閱讀《提升生產力的6大時間追蹤應用程式》。

只是要記住,那篇文章裡列出的應用程式清單絕不是完整清單。

「Damon,我要如何運用我的數據來提升生產力?」

這是個好問題。數據除非拿來使用,否則毫無價值。

我來解釋一下我的做法。你或許可以直接套用到自己的流程中,或者需要稍作調整。無論如何,這都是一個起點。

我追蹤的其中一項數據,是我寫一篇部落格文章需要多少時間。假設一個月下來,我發現要花2小時,這包括研究、撰寫、編輯、發布內容,以及找一張合適的配圖。

所以我有了這些數據,接下來呢?

首先,我喜歡挑戰自己。所以我會試著在1小時55分鐘內寫完一篇部落格文章。如果能持續做到,我就把它當作新的基準,再試著縮短到1小時50分鐘。

你應該懂這個道理了。

第二,我把數據當作截止期限來用。

我不會讓計時器在我寫文章時往上累加,而是設定為2小時,讓它倒數。計時器就放在我面前,我能看著秒數和分鐘數一點點流逝。

這對我來說很有激勵作用。如果進度落後,我就會加快速度,確保能在期限內完成。

第三件我用數據做的事,是追蹤我一整週的時間分配。

我喜歡從宏觀的角度檢視自己的產出。如果我把70%的寫作時間都花在部落格上,那就代表我沒有投入足夠的時間去寫Kindle書籍和其他資訊產品。

你能用同樣的方式運用你的數據嗎?這取決於你的工作方式和你正在追求的目標。但現在你知道我是怎麼做的了。

這封信已經太長了,就先在這裡收尾。關於時間追蹤,我還有很多話想說,但那可以留到以後再談。

現在,關於這個主題,我能給你最重要的建議就是:今天就開始追蹤你的時間。不要等待,現在就開始培養這個習慣。

如果你一定要用線上應用程式來做這件事,記得去看看我部落格上介紹的前5名(以我個人看法)。

如果你最終使用了那篇文章中提到的任何應用程式,告訴我你的看法。

好的、壞的、醜陋的都可以說。

無論如何,我們幾天後再聊。

如果你也受夠了當一個資訊癮君子,你一定會喜歡我最近寫的一篇部落格文章,標題是《避免資訊超載的簡單系統》。

emails.subject: The bad habit that cost me $100,000
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Damon here.

Bad habits are expensive. You know this.

But there's one habit that's really devious: information gluttony.

Tell me if this sounds familiar...

You want to perform a specific task, but don't know how to do it. So you visit Google and start typing away. Within seconds, you're presented with a ton of pages that promise to walk you through the steps.

Jackpot! So far, so good.

That's when things go downhill.

You click to the first page. It looks good, but you're afraid of missing out on something important.

So you hit the back button on your browser and click to the second page. It too looks good. But because you want to do the job right the first time, you go back to Google and look at next several pages.

And you start bookmarking everything. That way, you can easily find the information later.

Congratulations. You've become an info glutton.

Before you know it, two hours have slipped by and you still haven't accomplished the task you set out to learn.

Total waste of time.

I used to do that all the time. And it cost me at least $100,000.

Here's the story:

Way back in 2000, I wrote a book. It did pretty well, selling thousands of copies for $39 a pop.

Naturally, I got excited and started brainstorming ideas for another book. I also began researching how to promote the first book more effectively. (I stunk at promotion.)

Can you guess what happened?

I never stopped brainstorming and researching. By the time I had settled on an idea for the second book, two years had floated by. I missed a huge window of opportunity to capitalize on the idea.

It gets worse.

Over that same 2-year time frame, I never managed to launch a promotion campaign for my first book. Sales eventually dwindled to a trickle.

Meanwhile, a few friends of mine were running the same type of business: writing and selling books. While I spent two years in "research mode," my friends had released several new products.

Sales were cranking for them. To the tune of six figures per year.

That's how being an information glutton cost me at least $100,000.

Can you relate? Do you find yourself researching things and never taking action? Believe me, I get it.

In my next email, I'll show you how to break this habit into a million tiny pieces.

Until then,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. If you're not reading my blog, check it out. I cover strategies that will help you save time, generate income and carve out a more rewarding lifestyle from the same 24 hours you have now.
emails.contentZh:

emails.subject: 張振輝, are you losing time?
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

How's getting up early in the morning working for you so far? Let me know whenever you get the chance.

Let's keep moving forward...

This is going to be a short email. But it's an important one.

On page 10 of Catapult Your Productivity! I gave you a simple tip that will help you regain control of your workday.

Here it is in a nutshell:

Track. Your. Time.

It doesn't matter what you're doing. Unless you're monitoring how much time it takes you to finish, you're spending too much of it. Time is slipping through your fingers.

Here's a personal example:

I create content for a handful of clients. I'm talking about articles, blogs, newsletters, white papers, etc.

For one particular client, I write some pretty in-depth articles. Each one used to take me 3 hours to research, write, edit and deliver.

Today, those articles take 1 hour and 20 minutes apiece.

Think about that for a minute. I'm saving 1 hour and 40 minutes per article for this client. That's a big deal!

How did I do it?

Simple. I started tracking my time. I literally sat down with a kitchen timer and kept my eye on it while writing. I watched as the minutes ticked away.

Here's the really dumb thing: prior to tracking my time, I didn't realize each article was taking me 3 hours to complete. I was unwittingly allowing time to slip through my fingers.

Stupid.

So I bought myself a little timer and voila! My productivity went through the roof.

And the kicker? According to my client, my writing style actually improved.

Here's your homework for today: buy yourself a timer. Put it on your desk and track how long it takes you to complete certain tasks.

Write the numbers down.

You'll be floored by how much time is slipping through your fingers. Now's your chance to reclaim it!

In a few days, I'll share a personal story about a bad habit that has cost me over $100,000. You may be suffering from it too.

Stay tuned!

Damon Zahariades

P.S. If you must use an online timer, check out Toggl.com. It's free and drop-dead simple to use.

P.P.S. Looking for a way to boost your daily output? Check out my Kindle book The Time Chunking Method: A 10-Step Action Plan For Increasing Your Productivity.

emails.subject: The simple 4-step system to getting up earlier...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

It's Damon.

A couple days ago, I told you how the simple habit of getting up early and digging into work without wasting time improved my life. I encouraged you to try it and let me know how it went.

Today, I was going to share a simple tip you can use to squeeze even more juice out of your workday.

But I'm going to put that tip on ice for a day or two.

Why? Because several people emailed me to say they were having trouble getting out of bed an hour earlier than normal.

I understand. I get it. It's one thing to read about doing it. It's another thing to actually DO it!

Once you train your brain to get up at a certain time each morning, it's hard to move that time forward.

Your brain is a creature of habit.

So today, I'm going to give you a simple 4-step action plan for getting up early. Fair warning: it won't be easy. But it WILL work.

Here it is...

Step 1: Set your alarm clock 15 minutes earlier than normal.

One of the "secrets" to forming a new habit is to do it slowly. After 2 or 3 days, set your alarm clock back another 15 minutes.

Or 10 minutes if you're a wimp (just kidding).

Step 2: Put your alarm clock (or phone) 10 feet away from your bed.

We both know how tempting it is to hit snooze. It's only a few extra minutes, so what the big deal, right?

The big deal is that hitting snooze trains your brain to expect it. That's the opposite of what we're trying to do here.

By putting your alarm clock 10 feet away from your bed, you're forcing yourself to get up. By the time you walk over to your clock, you won't be nearly as motivated to hit snooze.

After all, you're already up. You may as well get dressed and start your day.

By the way, I mention this tip on page 8 of my ebook Catapult Your Productivity! Hopefully, you've read it.

Step 3: Down 16 ounces of water.

Drinking water will wake you up. I'm not sure why. But it works.

Step 4: Hit the sack when you're sleepy.

Don't sabotage yourself by going to bed late. Getting up early doesn't mean you can shortchange yourself on the front-end. If you're feeling drowsy, turn off the TV and go to bed.

I'm not saying the action plan above is easy. Changing habits is always a challenge. Remember, your brain is a creature of habit. It's going to put up a fight.

But if you stick with it, you'll definitely win the fight. That's when you'll start seeing a huge boost in your daily output.

Want a few more tips on becoming an early riser? I've got just the thing for you...

Read this blog post ===> http://www.artofproductivity.com/how-to-become-an-...

That's it for today. Short 'n sweet.

If you're having trouble dragging yourself out of bed each morning, use the 4-step action plan I've laid out above. It takes discipline. But it works.

I guarantee it.

And be sure to read this blog post for more good stuff on this topic.

In a couple days, I'll share that tip I was going to give you today. You may already be using it. If not, you'll definitely want to open that email!

Talk soon,

Damon Zahariades

Author of The Time Chunking Method, The 30-Day Productivity Plan, and other time management and productivity books

P.S. If you know someone who's having trouble getting up early, forward this email to them. Or just send them a link to the blog post.
emails.contentZh:
嘿 張振輝,

我是Damon。

前幾天,我告訴過你,早起並立刻投入工作、不浪費時間這個簡單的習慣,如何改變了我的人生。我鼓勵你試試看,並告訴我結果如何。

今天,我原本打算跟你分享一個能讓你從工作日榨出更多效益的簡單技巧。

但我打算把那個技巧先擱置一兩天。

為什麼?因為有好幾個人寫信告訴我,他們很難比平常早一小時起床。

我理解,我懂。閱讀怎麼做是一回事,真正去「做」又是另一回事!

一旦你訓練大腦每天在特定時間起床,要把那個時間提前就會很困難。

你的大腦是習慣的產物。

所以今天,我要給你一套簡單的4步驟早起行動計畫。先提醒你:這不會容易,但一定「有效」。

以下就是這套計畫……

第1步:把鬧鐘設定得比平常早15分鐘。

養成新習慣的「秘訣」之一,就是慢慢來。過了2、3天後,再把鬧鐘往前調15分鐘。

如果你是個膽小鬼,調10分鐘也行(開玩笑的)。

第2步:把鬧鐘(或手機)放在離床10英尺遠的地方。

我們都知道按下貪睡鍵有多誘人,反正只是多睡幾分鐘,有什麼大不了的,對吧?

問題就在於,按貪睡鍵會訓練你的大腦期待這麼做,而這正好和我們想達成的目標相反。

把鬧鐘放在離床10英尺遠的地方,能強迫你起床。等你走到鬧鐘旁邊時,你按貪睡鍵的動力已經沒那麼強了。

畢竟你已經起來了,不如就換好衣服,開始你的一天。

順帶一提,我在電子書《催化你的生產力!》第8頁提到過這個技巧,希望你已經讀過了。

第3步:喝下16盎司的水。

喝水會讓你清醒過來。我不確定原因是什麼,但確實有效。

第4步:感到睏了就去睡覺。

不要因為太晚睡而破壞自己的計畫。早起不代表你可以在前一晚虧待自己。如果覺得睏了,就關掉電視去睡覺。

我不是說上面這套行動計畫很容易,改變習慣永遠是個挑戰。記住,你的大腦是習慣的產物,它會反抗。

閱讀這篇部落格文章 ===> http://www.artofproductivity.com/how-to-become-an-...

今天就到這裡,簡短扼要。

如果你每天早上都很難把自己從床上拖起來,就用我上面列出的4步驟行動計畫吧。這需要紀律,但確實有效。

我保證。

也一定要閱讀這篇部落格文章,裡面有更多關於這個主題的精彩內容。

過幾天,我會分享今天原本要給你的那個技巧。你可能已經在用了,如果沒有,你一定會想打開那封信!

再聊,

Damon Zahariades

《時間分塊法》、《30天生產力計畫》及其他時間管理與生產力書籍作者

emails.subject: Here's a drop-dead simple productivity hack...
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

Damon here.

Last time, I gave you a homework assignment.

I wanted you to crack open Catapult Your Productivity! - the free ebook I sent you a couple days ago - and read the first two habits.

Here they are:

Habit #1: Wake up early
Habit #2: Start working immediately upon waking

I also promised you a story. That story shows how huge an impact these two habits can have on your life.

Here it is...

In 2004, I quit my day job. I was making triple my salary with my side business. (I'll go into more detail about that in another email.) So sticking around seemed like a waste of time.

Let me tell you, the great thing about making a ton of money with very little effort is that you can do pretty much anything you want.

The bad thing is that it makes you lazy. It also dulls your edge so you're unprepared if your business goes sideways.

That's exactly what happened to me.

But I'm getting ahead of myself. Let's get back to 2004.

I'm suddenly unemployed and making more money than I know what to do with.

Here's what life was like prior to 2004...

4:00 a.m. - get out of bed and work on my side business.
6:00 a.m. - get showered and dressed. Hit the local Starbucks to work online (promote my book and write my weekly newsletter).
8:00 a.m. - arrive at the office.
5:30 p.m. - leave the office and head home.
6:00 p.m. - grab some dinner and get to work on my side business.
11:00 p.m. - wind down with an episode of X-Files (my favorite TV series)
12:00 a.m. - hit the sack

I used to drink a ton of coffee. No doubt it helped me to function. But it was totally unhealthy. Seriously. I don't recommend it.

Things changed dramatically when I quit my day job.

Here's what life was like after 2004...

10:00 a.m. - drag myself out of bed.
10:30 a.m. - check email, check business numbers, read news (CNN.com, NYTimes.com, etc.).
11:00 a.m. - hit the coffee shop, grab lunch and hang out with friends.
2:30 p.m. - return home. Do a little work on my side business.
5:00 p.m. - call it a day. Call some friends, play video games or go to Starbucks.
10:00 p.m. - watch television or play video games with friends.
2:30 a.m. - hit the sack.

Pretty huge difference, right? I did a complete 180° when I quit my job. I went from being a productivity machine to a complete sloth.

And here's what happened as a result...

My business slowly cratered. So did my income. Month by month, I made less and less.

At first, I didn't give it much thought. I was making way more money than I needed to make my nut. So making a little less than I did the previous month didn't bother me.

It should have.

Remember when I said getting lazy dulls your edge? It dulls it to the point that you're unprepared if things go sideways.

That was me in a nutshell.

Over the course of two and a half years, my massive income dipped to the salary I was making at the corporate job I quit in 2004. Within 6 more months, it plummeted below that line.

I was in big trouble.

Let's stop here for a moment.

Can you guess why my business failed? Here's a hint: it has a lot to do with the first two habits I talk about in Catapult Your Productivity!

Habit #1: Wake up early
Habit #2: Start working immediately upon waking

After I quit my job, my productivity went through the floor. First, I got up late each morning. Second, I made matters worse by pushing work aside for several hours.

I had dug a hole that was so deep, clawing my way out seemed impossible. So I made a big change. I decided to wake up early each morning, weekends included, and dig into work right off the bat.

No more wasting time. No more acting like a tree sloth.

Guess what happened.

I started a new business and it took off. I also started writing again. I began making a lot more money and now have several books published and more in the works.

Here's the lesson...

You can do hundreds of things to boost your productivity. But you've got to start somewhere.

My advice? Start by creating the first two habits I cover in Catapult Your Productivity! You'll be absolutely floored by how much it can improve your life.

But don't take my word for it. Give it a shot and see for yourself. Then, shoot me a quick email to let me know how it worked out for you.

I got a little longwinded in this email. That's what happens when I tell a story.

Here's your "homework" for the next couple of days: get up an hour earlier and start tackling the items on your to-do list.

That's it.

Shoot me an email and tell me how it goes.

In a couple days, I'm going to share a tip with you that will completely change the way you look at your work day. Guaranteed.

Talk to you then,

Damon Zahariades

跟你說,不費多少力氣就能賺進大把鈔票,最棒的地方就是你幾乎可以做任何想做的事。

但壞處是,它會讓你變得懶惰,也會磨鈍你的敏銳度,讓你在事業出狀況時毫無防備。

而這正是發生在我身上的事。

不過我扯遠了,讓我們回到2004年。

我突然失業了,但賺的錢多到我不知道該怎麼花。

以下是2004年之前我的生活作息……

凌晨4:00 - 起床,開始經營我的副業。
上午6:00 - 洗澡穿衣,到附近的星巴克上網工作(宣傳我的書,寫每週電子報)。
上午8:00 - 抵達辦公室。
下午5:30 - 離開辦公室回家。
下午6:00 - 吃點晚餐,繼續處理副業。
晚上11:00 - 看一集《X檔案》(我最愛的電視劇)放鬆一下。
凌晨12:00 - 上床睡覺。

我以前喝很多咖啡,無疑這幫助我撐了下去,但真的很不健康。說真的,我不推薦這麼做。

當我辭掉正職工作後,一切都徹底改變了。

以下是2004年之後我的生活作息……

上午10:00 - 勉強把自己從床上拖起來。
上午10:30 - 查看電子郵件、檢查生意數字、看新聞(CNN.com、NYTimes.com等)。
上午11:00 - 到咖啡店吃午餐,跟朋友聚聚。
下午2:30 - 回家,稍微處理一下副業。
下午5:00 - 收工。打電話給朋友、打電動或去星巴克。
晚上10:00 - 看電視或跟朋友打電動。
凌晨2:30 - 上床睡覺。

差別相當大吧?辭職後我來了個180度大轉變,從一台生產力機器變成一隻徹頭徹尾的樹懶。

結果發生了這樣的事……

我的事業逐漸崩潰,收入也是。一個月接著一個月,我賺得越來越少。

一開始我沒太在意,因為我賺的錢遠遠超過我維持生計所需,所以比上個月少賺一點也不會困擾我。

但這其實應該要讓我在意才對。

還記得我說過懶惰會磨鈍你的敏銳度嗎?它會磨鈍到你在事情出狀況時毫無防備的地步。

那正是當時的我。

經過兩年半的時間,我原本豐厚的收入,跌到只剩我2004年辭去的那份公司工作的薪水水準。再過6個月,更是跌破了那條線。

我陷入了大麻煩。

先在這裡停一下。

你猜得出我的事業為什麼失敗嗎?這裡給你一個提示:這跟我在《催化你的生產力!》裡談到的前兩個習慣有很大關係。

習慣一:早起
習慣二:一起床就立刻開始工作

辭職之後,我的生產力一落千丈。首先,我每天早上都起得很晚;其次,我還把工作往後拖延好幾個小時,讓情況更糟。

我挖了一個深不見底的洞,爬出來似乎是不可能的任務。於是我做出了重大改變:我決定每天早起,週末也不例外,並且一起床就立刻投入工作。

不再浪費時間,不再像隻樹懶一樣。

猜猜後來發生了什麼事。

我開始了一個新事業,而它起飛了。我也重新開始寫作,開始賺到更多錢,現在已經出版了好幾本書,還有更多正在進行中。

這裡就是教訓所在……

你可以做上百件事來提升生產力,但你得先從某個地方開始。

我的建議?從培養我在《催化你的生產力!》裡提到的前兩個習慣開始。你一定會對它能為你的人生帶來多大的改善感到驚訝。

但別只聽我說,親自試試看,然後寫封簡短的信告訴我結果如何。

這封信寫得有點囉嗦,每次講故事都會這樣。

以下是你接下來幾天的「功課」:早起一個小時,開始處理待辦清單上的事項。

就這麼簡單。

寫封信告訴我進展如何。

過幾天,我會跟你分享一個技巧,徹底改變你看待工作日的方式,保證有效。

到時候再聊,

Damon Zahariades

emails.subject: Welcome aboard 張振輝
emails.contentEn:
Hey 張振輝,

First, congratulations for grabbing my ebook Catapult Your Productivity! The Top 10 Habits You Must Develop To Get More Things Done. You're going to love it!

In case you need the download link again, here it is.

Don't dismiss the ebook just because it's free. It's packed with 40+ pages of solid tips and strategies that will help you squeeze more value out of every day. I've paid for Kindle books that offer a lot less value than Catapult Your Productivity!

Over the next few weeks, I'm going to show you a bunch of ways to be more productive and live a more rewarding life. Think of how having three extra hours each day could change everything. You'd be able to...

- spend more quality time with your spouse
- hang out more often with your kids
- get together more frequently with your friends
- pursue your favorite hobby
- start a side business to earn a second income

You may already be using some of the tactics we're going to cover over the next few weeks. If so, that's fantastic! You're doing better than most folks.

But I guarantee you're also going to hear about strategies you've never considered.

A lot of what I'm going to share with you in these emails won't be available on my blog. So definitely keep an eye out for them in your inbox.

Also, whenever I release a new Kindle book, I'm going to slash the price for a day or two. As a subscriber, you'll be the first to hear about it.

That's it for today. I don't want to overwhelm you with information. But here's what I'd like you to do right now:

Open "Catapult Your Productivity!" and read the beginning, along with the first 2 habits. Here's the download link again.

Next time, I'll share a personal story about how a stupid mistake related to those 2 habits negatively impacted my life.

I'll bet you'll be able to relate.

Let's talk in a day or two,

Damon Zahariades

P.S. If you don't want to receive these tips from me, feel free to unsubscribe at the link below. I only want you here if you truly want to be here!

P.P.S. If you need actionable tips on how to get more done right now, be sure to check out my books.
